div.p: gottrg.

A SORE TRIAL TRIP. . Oh, the seas how they roar ! Stormy winds how they blow! While we Dolphin sailor boys are working on the mast, And the land-lubbers lying down below, below, below! With the land-lubbers lying down below! Three times to sea went our gallant Dolphin ship; Three times and out went she! And a stout little tug towed her back into the slip, i With a hot box, melted journal, jammed screw, broken shaft, slipped eccentric, : . Collapsed flue, choked mud-valve, cylinder-heads blown out, governor thrown off, safety-valve clogged, rudder unshipped, And her bob-stayshanging where her spanker ought to be, Rack aft, where her spanker ought to be. R. J. Btrunarrn, in Brooklyn Eagle. .. - ...• -

MERMAID'S CAVE. 0 rushing wave, Flow past the seaward cliff, the-broken shore, And in the deep recesses of the cave Call the sea-nymphs once more! Is it so long Since here they sat, with pearl and amber wreathed, And to the sea, that loved than well, a song Of kindred rapture breathed? - A thousand years! bat is that to Ocean's memory !

But w) Still from the cliff drop slow the misty tears Of the unchanging sea. Still ebb and flow, Seeking and calling with perpetual moan, Though but the sea-flowers in the twilight glow And give no answering tone! • With every breeze Send forth a message, southward, westward blown; Tell them pink-petaled, bright anemones • ' Have in their foot-prints grown. And some soft day 11)f rich midsummer may tie wanderers bring, In this dim grotto evermore to stay, Beloved of Ocean's King. —Harper's Monthly. FRANCES L. MACE.

_ We want to ask one question—" Can a person go round a square 2 It is very true that charity shouldbegin at home, This is the Divine order. But if it ends there, it is not true -charity, or love, but selfishness. Let a man have such a heart as the the Son of God describes in the beatitudes, and a whole universe of sor- row cannot rob him of his blessedness. A health journal says that a cold may be cured if the patient will eat nothing for a day or two. In case no relief comes in that time, continue the treatment. The following advertisement appeared in a French paper Wanted a distinguished and healthy-looking man to be cured patient' in a doctor's waiting-room. _
—Address," arc. Science tells us that after a bee has stung once it takes two minutes to recover the power to sting again. It doesn't take the stung person two seconds to get out of

1:1;;;:ay of a second sting. "Fray of what did your brother die?" inquired the Marquis of Spinola of Sir Horace Vere. "He died, sir," replied he, "of having nothing to do." "Al is sir," said Spinola, "that is enough to kill any General of us all." "John is very kind to the poor," said Mary, "but:after aU, it may be more for the sake of praise than:doing good." Look here, Mary, said her husband, "when you see the hands of our clock always right, you may be sure that there isn't much wrong with the inside works." Hostess: "Are you a musician, Mr. Sissy ?" Mr. Sissy (who is dying to give an exhibition of his ability): I Well--er—yes, I think I can lay claim to some know- ledge of music." Hostess: "I am delighted to know it. My daughter is about to play, and I would be very glad if you would kindly turn the music for her." It is sad but true that however tyrannical and over- bearing a man may be in public, there is oftenla thin- lipped and silent woman in his home in whose presence he feels as cheap as a last year's almanac, and before whom he would no more think of putting on frills than he would dare to ask her to sing a comic song.

-- We are like children in our-poor unreason, As we reach after joys That at the best can please but for a season, And then are broken toys. If we would only walk the paths of duty, Humbly and with thanksgiving, Our hearts would learn in lessons full of beauty.' ; An attendant at Mount Vernon, not long ago, found a lidy weeping most bitterly and audibly, with her Fa dkerchief at her eyes. Be slipped up to her and sai 1: "Are you in trouble, madam'?" "No, sir," she sobbed. "I saw you weeping." " Ah," said she, how can one help weeping at the grave of the 'Father of I his Country'?" "Oh, indeed, madam," said he, "that' not it. The tomb's over yonder. This is the ice-house.': Sheridan agreed with Walker that the pronunciation of wind should be wynde, but insisted, contrary to Walker, that .gold should be goold. Mr. Sheridan tells us that Swift used to jeer those who pronounced wind with a short "i," by saying, "I have a great minn'd to ftnn'd why you prondUnce it winn'd." Au illiberal critic retorted this upon Mr. Sheridan by saying, "If I may be so boold, I should be glad to be toold:whyyou pronounce

it goold." It is in no sense a part of an American Minister's duty to act as social sponsor for ambitious nobodies, or 1 to introduce at Court people who do not know:how to behave when they get there. A once too-easily per- suaded Minister yielded to the teasing of one of his countrywomen and presented her at thegourt of one of the Continental nations. The Queen received her most kindly, but judge of the Minister's horror when, tol Her Majesty's kindly welcome, the American woman replied, "I really feel as if I had known you'allong:time ; :you know, we go to the same chiropodist." Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, who wrote most execrable verses, was so enraged at the opinion of Philo- w,ho declared them to be wretched,' that he sent him to prison. Next morning, being supplicated by his friends, he released him, and invited him the same night to a magnificent banquet. Here the tyrant recited some , ranting nonsense of his own composition, and, turning round, asked Philolenes what he thought of it. The other, without giving any reply, called to Dionysius's myrmidons, and said, "Lead me to prison." The tyrant could not restrain a laugh, and pardoned him. . Horace Smith told a good story of a night he had -passed in a stage-coach. The four inside passengers had -naturally endeavoured to settle themselves as comfort- 'ably as circumstances would permit. Two of:them were a married couple, the husband sitting with his back to the horses, and evidently not altogether at his:ease. About half an hour after starting he turned to his wife and anxiously inquired if she was comfortable. "Pretty well," she replied, in a drowsy tone. "You feel no draught from the window ?" 'None at all." "Quite sure?" "Quite." "Ah," remarked the affectionate spouse, "then suppose we change places." The Colonel of an Alabama regiment, which. served during the Rebellion, was famous for having everything done in military style. Once, while field-officer of the day, going on his tour of inspection, he came upon a sentinel sitting on the ground, with Ids gun entirely to pieces. The following dialogue then :took :place:— Colonel: "Don't you -know that a sentinel, while on duty, should always keep on his feet ?" Sentinel (with- out looking up) : "That's the way we used to do when the war began; but that's outlawed long ago." Colonel (beginning to doubt if the man was really on duty) : Are you the sentinel here?" Sentinel: "Well, I'm a sort of a sentinel." Colonel: "Well, I'm a sort of officer of the day." Sentinel: "Well, if you'll hold on till I sort of git my, gun together, I'll give you a sort of salute." CHRISTINE NILSSON AND THE QuEEN.—One,:of the pre- sents she prizes most came from her Majestfthe Queen, who heard Madame Nilsson at Windsor, and with her own hands pat a bracelet of rubies and diamonds on her wrist, to which a little story is attached, The :fact is that Madame Nilsson had been asked by some nuns who keep a school for poor girls if she woula be so extremely kind as to ding once to those little ones, as it would make an impression on them which they would never forget. Madame Nilsson, too happy to do so much good with so little trouble, promised to come, and fixed a certain even- ing. But what should happen but a visitor, under the guise of her Majesty's bandmaster, called on Madame /Clasen, the bearer of her Majesty' g order for Madame Nilsson to sing at the Court concert at Buckingham Palace. Of course, you suppose that she instantly sent to the nuns to express her regret not to be able to sing to the children that night on account of the Court con- cert? -Not she! She told her Majesty's bandmaster that she was very sorry not to be able to accept the Queen's invitation for that evening, as she had an en- gagement which she could not evade; and that at any future opportunity she would be happy to receive her Majesty's command, but that she could not, sing at Court that evening. "Not obey the Queen's command? Not sing at Court? Why, every artist coming to London desired, before all, the honour of being invited to Court 2" What was he to do? That "was his concern," Madame Nilsson said; she could not break her word. Trembling returned the messenger, revolving in his mind how he would lay before her Majesty the message that Madame Nilsson liad something else to do. However, there was no mincing matters ;he had to say- it. But what was his astonishment when, instead of the Royal frown he Mooted, he heard the august lady say," oh, I know— know. I have been told what that engagement is, and right noble heart she has! Put Madame Nilsson down at once for the next Court concert, and ask her what day she can give me the pleasure of singing to me per- sonally at Windsor." Fleet, like a deer, to Madame Nilsson returned the Royal courier to take her orders ; and thus Madame Nilsson was invited to Windsor, and by Royal hands adorned with the bracelet above men- tioned.—Temple Bar. bias. 8. DEAR FRED,—You will be arapnaea at receivirqg a letter from me, but thank God, I am pleatibd to say.l am getting better every day. I sball be is 'glad to breathe the fresh air 'gain It has seemed a dreadful Long lime to be in bed. You know 1 was taken tn the Hospital last April to pe treated for laight's Mamie ot the Kidneys. Well, on the 31st of July they tapped me, and took away 301 ounces of water. The same thing was done again Co the 18th September, and u 8 ounces of water obtained. On the 9th October I was discharged from the Hospital as incurable. In Janu- ary this year (the 20112), was again tapped at home and 330 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bar- tholomew's Hospital in London refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Bartholomew's Hospital, Chath on. also refused ins, as being the worst case tney had seen for years, and two local doctor. gave me , up as hopeless. When I came from the Hosp'tal it to lc three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was en object of ml .ery and despair. After the Hospitals had refused me and doctors given me up. my wife persuaded me to try Hop Bide, s, and from he commencement have improved daily. I have only. taken them seven weeks and can now get deism- stairs and wallc about without even a stick. With the aid f a few more bottles of the bitters shall be wail again. The water has entirely left my body and legs. The on'y trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful issedicine. I wish I had tried It sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with d 'Moss' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the Hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind that so long as lam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is near, for everyone had given me up a.a bad job. With best wishes to . . . . . . I remain, your affect'onate Brother. The finest load of steers seen at the Chicago Yards, came all the way from Memphis, Tenn. Although they averaged only 1,2701b5., they found a buyer at 5 dole. '55 cents. They were bought for the English market. The famous Holstein cow Baide which had given as high as 931bs. of milk per day, and was owned by B. B. Lord and Son, of Sinclairville, N.Y., died recently. They had refused an offer of 1,700 dols. for the cow. A report of fruit products in the Clyde district states that apples and pears show promise of an unusually abundant yield, while plums and berries of most kinds will be only a fair crop, and in some cases. much below the average. Clouds of smoke are used in the French vineyards as a protection against frost. A new method of producing the smoke is to mix gas tar with sawdust and Old straw. Placed in heaps, this mixture remains imflanansable for ' weeks, in spite of wet weather. Dense clouds of smoke decrease radiation from the ground, and so counteract frost, which is most injurious to the vines. Tits DAIRYMAN.—Mr. T. D. Curtis says the true-dairy- man must not only know if good cow when he sees her, but how to feed and care for her, and how to handle her milk and manufacture the product. He must be intelli- gent, cleanly, systematic, and thorough, and do every- thing at the right tithe and in the right place, "decently and in order.' The demand for educated dairymen is increasing, and will continue to increase for many ~years. A STORY or QllSBEC.—Passing through St. Louis Gate, with its new Norman turrets, we have to our right the winding ascent to the Citadel and to our left the Esplan- ade; while at the corner of the St. LiSuid Hotel we are again in the business centre of the upper town, and soon come to the open area of the Place d'Armes, whence we pass into Buade-street, on which stands the new Post Office, a handsome building of grey cut-stone, plain but in good taste, with two short lonic pillars at the entrance. The old Post Office which preceded it had a history, symbolised by a French inscription under the sign of the Chien d'Or, or Golden Dog, which legendary animal still retains his post over the entrance of the pre- sent building. This inscription was the expression of the wrongs suffered by the original owner—a merchant named Philibert—at the hands of the Intendant Bigot of unsavoury memory. The legend may be freely trans- lated, "I bide my time." Poor Philibert was never able to put his threat into execution, his life and his plans for revenge being suddenly brought to an end on a dey on Mountain Hill, by a sword thrust from a French officer, no doubt at the Intendant's .instigation. The story had a sequel, however. Philibert's brother, who came all the way from Bordeaux as his executor and blood avenger, tracked the assassin to his refuge in the East Indies and slew him there.—Front " Picturesque Canada" for June. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA. to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— aldra;

EUROPEAN ARMY AND NAVY EATIMATRS —During 1884 the army and navy estimates of the nations of Europe amoanted to £lB3 519,997, while the national debts ab- sorbed £207,431,825 for interest alone, the aggregate na- tional debt reaching to £4,602389,941. In view of these figures, all will agree with Mr. Bright that the crushing weight of the military systems of Europe cannot be sup- ported indefinitely with patience. At the head of the list stands Russia, whose army and navy estimates amounted to £48.102.500, and the interest on her national debt to £33,180026. Republican France comes next. Her army and navy estimates were £33.730,783, and the interest on her national debt £44,4.35,236, he haying the largest na- tional debt in Europe. Next to France stands our own country, with army and navy estimates amounting to £31,420,755, with a payment for interest on the national debt of £29,879,098. Our entire national debt stood in 1884 at £758,180,936. The army and navy estimates of the German empire were £22,624749, while the interest on the national debt (including the German States) amounted to £14,152,558. In point of expenditure Italy follows Ger- many, that country's estimates for army and navy being ,E 12,055,589 and the interest on her national debt 1Z21,088,623. Next in importance is Austro-Hongary, with army and navy estimates amounting to £13,413,795, and the Interest on the national debt to £25,613,923,

Faun CROPS.—Raspberries are as usual a heavy crop, and the raM we are having Was much needed to swell the earliest fruit, as well as to cleanse some of the other fruit trees, The raspberry, so far as we are aware, has not had a single insect enemy to obstruct its progress. It is true that birds are tempted to destroy the fruit as fast as it colours, but if protected from these feathered thieves, we do not know of a more profitable crop. In- tending planters should keep a sharp look-out for the best varieties. The time to do this is when the fruit is ripe. There is no comparison between those we gener- ally see lip old gardens and the bes,t varieties now in cul- tivation. Bush fruits—which include the various sorts of currants and gooseberries—are a good crop where the birds have not interfered with the buds in the spring. Currant trees have, however, during the past five days become infested with aphis, which will have a tendency to diminish the weight of the crop, as it cannot swell to its full-size if the bulk of the leaves fail to perform their functions. 'The gooseberry, and frequently the currant, exceptlthe black ones, are about this time of the year subject to visitation by a caterpillar or the larwe of the ma i gpie moth, which n a few days will devour the leaves so that nothing remains but the petiole. When it has troubled us we have tried most of the prescribed re- medies, but none of them proved so effectual as one would Wish, The remedy, whatever it is must be in- stantaneous to be of mucn value, as hundreds of leaves will be stripped off one tree in a few hours. Powdered hellebore was the best preventive,tut rather too ex- pensive; but still worth carrying out where a few trees only are cultivated. Shaking the trees and dusting newly-slaked lime over the fallen catterpillars was only partially effectual, for in a few minutes they foundltheir way up the tree to resume their destructive operations. We found road dust as effectual as anything; not in de- stroying the insect, of course, but in making every;bite unpleasant, for the leaves are actually eaten, but are not relished with a layer of grit on them. So the caterpillar quits them, as it will not remain many minutes in a place unless it can be eating. The best method of applying the dust to the trees is to wet them, so that it may ad- here, as soon as the caterpillar makes its appearance, and not wait for rain or heavy dew. Ducks will devour the insect, and if they are conducted to the trees, and the latter receive a good shake, most of the insects will fall, and hundreds will soon be picked up by the ducks. THE FRowr Gsimax.—Cuttings or pipings of pinks should be put in at once either m pots or in a prepared patch of ground in a shady corner. Where only a fed' are required: the pot system is the best. Prepare the pots by placing an inch of drainage in the bottom of a 4-inch pot, and over this some of the rougher portion of the soil or half decayed leaves, to prevent the finer soil mingling with the crocks and obstructing the free pass- age of water. Over these some moderately fine, light, sandy soil should be put and slightly pressed. Into this the cuttings may be inserted so thick that their tops nearly touch. Many will strike roots if the pots are placed in a thoroughly shady corner, but all would do so if they could be covered with glass. A very simple contrivance could be made by fixing two layers of briek and a square or squares of glass on the top. If pots are dispensed with, enclose a patch of ground with bricks laid edgeways, and remove two inches of the top soil and replace it with some similar to that recommended for pots; after the cuttings are put in and watered, cover them over with glass. Boxes may be made for this and similar purposes without either tip or bottom, and they occupy much less space than bricks, and if coveredwith glass make excellent propagating frames. The cuttings should be selected from the strongest growths, and the two lowest pairs of leaves should be cut with a sharp knife as well as the portion of old wood at the base. We have succeeded in striking these by inserting them in the soil as they have been slipped off the parent plant, but they give more trouble, and it is almost im- possible to make them appear upright. _ Tog Wnwow.—As the weather is now it would be a pity to harbour any of the plants inside for any length of time. At any rate they should all be placed outside during showery weather, which will promote health and vigour, and the plants in a few hours will look fresh and clean. Double geraniums do not approve of too much wet at the time the trusses are well advanced. The pips or florets are so closely packed and absorbent that when once soaked the water is some time escaping, and if the sun shines on them in that state they are apt to be scalded and they very soon decay. When any of the florets appear to be injured or show symptoms of decay they should be moved, and those left—which are gener- ally plentiful—regulated to fill the vacant space.

GREAT EXCITEMENT IN WALES ABOUT A MARVELLOUS CURE. LIVING SIX YEARS WITHOUT GOING TO BED. Mr. FDITOR.—WhiIe spending a few days at the pleasant seaside town of' Aberystwlth, Cardiganshire, Wales, I heard related what seemed to me either a fabulous story or a mar- vellous cure.

The story PI as that a poor sufferer who had not been able to lie down in bed for six long Nears given up to die by all the Doctors, had been speedily cured by some Pattnt Medicine. It was related with the more implicit confidence from the circum- stance. as was said, that the Vicseof Lianrystyd was familiar with the facts, and could vouch for the truth of the report.

Having a little euricsity to know how such stories grow in travelling, / took the liberty while at the village of Llanrystyd to call upon the Vicars the Rev. T Evans, and to inquire abo this wonderful cure. Though a total stranger to him, both he and hls wife molt graciously entertained me in a ball hour's con- versation. principally touching the case of Mr. Yuji, in which they seemed to take a deep and sympatheic interest, having been familiar with his sufferings, and now rejoiced in what seeme to them a most remarkable cure. The Vicar remsrked that he presumed his name had been emnected with the report from his having mentioned the case to Mr. John Thomas, a chemist, of Llano's. He said Mr. Pugh was formerly a resident of their parish, but was now living ho the parish of Lianddeinol.

He strongly vouched for Mr. William Firth's character as a renpettable farmer and worthy of credit. I left the venerable Vicar wlto a livelier e‘ense of the happy relation of a pastor and people, feelimr that he was one who truly sympathised with all who are afil'eted in mlnd, body, or estate.

On my return to dberystwith, I was impreased with a desire to see Mr. Pugh, whose reputation stood so high. His farm Is called Pancom-Mawr, signifying •• above the dingle," situ- ated near the summit of a smooth round hill, event 4oking a baautiful valley in which is situated the lovely ivy mantled Church of Lianddeinol. I found Mr. Pugh, apparently about 40 years old, of medlam height, rather slight, with a pleasant and intelligent fore. I told him I had heard of his great Rifile- tiCal and of his remarkable and almost mirsculon. relief, and that I had come to learn from his own lips what thee was of truth in the reports.

-- --- Mr. Pugh remarked that his neighbours had taken a kindly and sympathetic Interest in his case for many years, but a late their interest had been greatly awakened by a happy change In his condition. What you report as having heard abroad, said he, is substantially true with one exception. I never under- stood that my ease was ever given up as hopeless by any phy- sTclan. I have been treated by several &eters hereabnuts, as good SS any In Wales, but unfortunately no prescription of theirs ever brought the desired relief.

Pilsen years ago, he said. I first became cm scious of a sour and deranged stomach and loss of appetite, which the doctors Lob' me was dyspepsia. What food I could hold in my st,mach seemed to no me no good, and was often thrown up with painful retching& This was followed after a time with hoarse- ness, and a raw soreness of the throat which the doctors caled bronchitis, and I was treated for that, but with little success. Then came shortness sf breath and a sense of suffocation, es- ppcially nigh's, with clammy sweat, and I would have to get, Oct of bed and sometimes open a door or window in winter weather to till my lungs with the cold air.

About six years ago I became so bad that I could not sleep In bed, but had to take my unquiet rest and dreamy sleep sitting in an armch4r. My affl'etion seemed to be working downward into my bowsls as well as upwards into my longs and throat. In the violent coughing spasms which grew more frequent, my abdomen would expand, and collar.se and at times it would seem that I should suffncate. All this time I was reduced :in strength so that I could perform no hard la- bour and my spirits were cm equently Much depressed. Ear'ry in this last spring I had a still more severe spasmodic attack, and my family and neighbours became alarmed, be- lieving that certainly I would not survive, when a neighbour. wits bad some knowledge, or had heard of the medicine sent 10 Aberystwitb by the driver of the Omnibus Post, som- seven mile distant, and fetched a bottlerd Mother Siegel's Curative Syrup. This medicine they administered to me according to the directions, when to their surprise and delight no less than soy own, the spasm ceased, I became at ease, and my sto- mach was calmed. My bowels were moved aa by a gentle cathartic, and I felt a sense of quiet comfort all through such as I had not before realised in many years. I could walk I around the house and breathe comfortably in a few hours after I had taken the medicine. I have continued to take the medl- I eine daily now for sorr ething over two months, and I can lay down and sleep sweetly at nights and have not since had a rr-currence of those terrible spasms and sweatings. I have been so long broken down and reduced in my whole system that I have not tried to perform any very hard out-door labow, deeming it hest to be prudent lest by over-exertion I may do myself injury before my strength is fully reanred. I feel that my stomach ri-d bowels have been and are being thoringhly renovated and renewed by the medicine. In fact I feel like a new man. div.p: After Lord Resebery had defended hie proposal at some length, the amendment of Lord Crenbrook was agreed to, and the clause as amended having lseen adopted without a division, the bill passed through Committee.—A bill to en- able the Ecclesiastical Commissioners to raise the salaries of archdeacons to £2OO a year was read a second time, on the motion of the PRIMATE. NAVAL EXPENDITURE.—The Earl of NORTHBROOK called attention to certaie statements relative to the administra- tion of the late Board of Admiralty, and declared that none of the charges made against him had any foundation in fact, pointing out that the Chancellor of the Exchequer had entirely avoided asking for information on the subject from the testy muscle: capable of giving detailed information las to how the Vote of Credit of April had been adreinis- tered. He invited the Government, if they had charges to bring against hint, to formulate them at once, and have them investigated by a tribunal consisting of a Joint Com- mittee of both houses, on which ex-First Lords of the Ad- miralty should vie—The Earl of HeanerentY remseked that the Chancellor of the Exchequer had not intended to make a personal atteck, but, finding that the sum stated as the I naval expendaure under the heading " special preparations" had been exteeded by a large amount. he could cot resist the conclusion that the department had been loosely adminis- I reed. It would be well that a Tarliamentary inquiry Ishould be instituted—The Earl of RAVAI;SWORTH ex- tressed hie; pleasure at the decision of the Government to institute -an inquiry into the lehject—The matter then dropped. Theit'lordships adjourned at eight o'cloele. HOUSE OF COMISM.NS.—TtrESDPLY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes to four O'CIOCE. QJ,C3TIONS, Lix.-1111%. S. &talent gave notice that on the first favourable opportunity he would ...neve that a Select Committee be appointed to inquire into the relative posi- tion of gold and silver and tneir use as money.—Mr. A. O'CIDNNOR asked why the letter or telegram of Lori 'Wel- seley to Sir Charles Wilson asking for explanations con- ceraing his delays was not included among the papers pre- sented to Parliamene—Mr. W. H. SMITH stated is eerily, that Lord Wolseley had not forwarded to the War °dice any matter addressed by him on the subject to Sir Charles Wilson.—ln reply to the Lord Mayor, Sir R. CROSS said : 'After careful consideration the Government had come to the conclusion that it would not be desirable to take pro- ceedings against the editor of the "Pall Mall Gazette." ENGLAND AND ATOHANHITAN.—Mr. BUCHARAN asked the Secretary for India whether Her Majesty's Government or the Government of India have entered into negotiations, or contemplate entering into negotiations, with the Ameer of Afghanistan. in order to form a military cantonment at or near Candahar, and whether they intend to take steps to- wards a military occupation of that place, with or without his Highness's consent.—Lord RANDOLPH CHVRCHILL said his reply to the iiret question was in the negative. As to whether the Government contemplated entering into nego- tiations, his answer to that was that he was not aware that any nezotiatione of that kind were contemplated. At the same time we were under certain pledges to the Ameer of Afghanistan, and if on account of these pledges it was necessary to aid in the defence of Candahare either in money or material, he imagined that, no matter what Government might be in power, the course of the British. Government would be clear. If they were to take steps for the occupa- tion of Cendahar without the consent of the Ameer, that would be an act of war, while at the present time the Ameer of Afghanistan was our friend and ally. . 'NATIONAL EDUCATION. The House went into Committee of Supply on the educa- tion estimates. Mr STANI,IOP3 moved for a grant of r 5,302722. RS against £3,182,875 last year, the increase being mostly required for the the better average attendance at day schools. The average cost per head in board schools last year was £2 Is 811, and in voluntary schools £1 15s 23, showing a differ- ence of 6s CA per head. It appeared, however, that the cost in London board schools affected the average in a large degree, being 12s 41 per scholar more than in voluntary schools, whereas in the provinces the difference between the two classes was only 3s lid, The total annual expenditure from all sources on popular education in the country was £6 451,000, exclusive of the sums laid out for building and enlarging schools. Since 1870 voluntary school buildings had cost £E,348.000, while school k Ards had borrowed 16,000,000 on the security of the rates. The capital ex- penditure on both classes for building purposes for the period indicated was about £23,000.000. Thera was now a total of school places for 4,826,000 children, against 4,337,000 on the books and 3,273,000 in average attend- ance. Oat of every hundred children in the whole country there were 96 on the books and 72 in average attendance. .

THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAI SHOW
A-T PRESTON.

On Tuesday morning at nine o'clock the imp7oment de- partment of the Royal Sh w, in Moor Park, wee opened. The weather was beautiful the beginning, and it has #lcon- tinued highly favourable al day. The ground is admirably adapted for the purposes of the, show in every department, and the manner in which the 'official structural arrange- ments have been carried oat is excellent. The principal entrance is within a stone-throw of the highway running north and south, and can be reached easily on foot and by conveyances, Sm., of which there is a most miscellaneous assortment now in activity. Tram cars likewise run close to the main entrance along the highway named. Sheds for machinery in motion flank the better half of the ground north and south; mechanism and an infinite variety of agricultural appliances occupy the ground inward in par- allel lines; the spaces reserved for live stock are at the eastern end of the park ; the quarters for the council, mem- bers of the society, dm., have a central position ; refresh- ment departments are towards the front or western end ; and up the centre of the land there Is a long, level, spacious avenue. Every part of the show can be reached easily. Immediately within and flanking the main entrance there are structural ranges most imposing fitted up, and in some respects quite "architecturally" attractive.. The erections in the quarter mentioned are occupied by exhibitors of agricultural, floral, and horticultural seeds, be' Messrs. Carter, of Reading: Sutton and Sons, London; Webb and Sons, Wordsley ; Oak- shott and Co., Reading; Dickson, Brown, and Tait, Man- chester; and Dickson and Sons, Chester. At each end there is a Canadian seed exhibition—one being the property of the Canadian Pacific Riilway Company, containing pro- ducts from Manitoba and other parts of North-Weat Canada, the country through which their lino runs prior to entering the Rocky Mountains; and the other belonging to the Dominion of Canada. Wth regard to the implements on the ground, or rather the exhibits iirthe department assigned for implements, they number in the aggregate 4,740. They are, of course, all up to the line of the latest inventive skill, but as compared with those exhilaitcl at last year's show of the Royal they do not include many actually new improve- ments; the mechanical progress manifested is rather in certain combinations and details than in anything of a dis- tinctly structural character. With respect to.the attendance at the show on Tuesday, it has not appeared to be so very large, but the area of the ground being so great—about ICO acres in extent—the actual number of visitors would seem less to the eye than it was in reality..

div.head: WELniE3DIiY.
div.p: WELniE3DIiY.

The show-yard was ca-a-e-n-tO-i-h-S-PUblic at eight o'clock. I when the judging of live stock, dairy produee, and poultry began. The weather, which on the previous day had been all that could be desired. was far from encouraging, and during the morning rain fell, though net heavily. There was a steady influx at visitors 'during the day, and it is estimated that the attendance waerquite up.to the average of previous years. Considerable interest was manifested in the displays of bee driving, Ar.c.,and lectures on bee manage- ment were given at frequent intervals during the afternoon. A. large number of visitors were attracted to the general exhibition of implements at rest and in motion. Tne work- ing dairy, which is designed to illustrate the English, French, and Danish methods of butter-making, was visited by a large number of persons during the day. The town has been most elaborately and artistically decorated, the principal streets being gay with 'flags and bunting. Mag- nificent triumphal arches span the roads at various points, and display symbols representing the loyal spirit of the people, and emblems of local significance, and legends ex- pressing a welcome to the Ro7al Agricultarel Society. Banners hang from almost every window, and royal standards, ensigns, and union jacks float from the roofs of most of the houses. The judging commenced about eight O'clock, and there would have been quite an average show of live stock but for a number of absentees, exhibitors from a distance failing to send forward their animals even to a greater extent than has been observable in many former isstances. This was especially the case in respect to Jerseys, there being about o a g ees : Sussex. Devon, and eleven! other breeds great many vacant stalls. The leading feature s decidedly the shorthorn, the.entries being 130, 3willndaitvlhan cattle ifseefi awnlesitr absentees than in some ef the other breeds. Herefords, ton, are larger in number than might have been expected, reaching 76 as catalogued. Out all did not come forward. The shorthorn old bull class brought a contest botween Mr. iiendlev's Self Esteem 2nd, Mr. Chapin in's Earl of Oxford from Cornwall, the Duke of Portland's Grand Ruth, and Mr. .1. T. Baker's Paulowi z, with the result that Mr. Handley' bull lost the pre•eminence it his held during the last three Royal shows, be only having second prize on this occasion, the pride of place going to the Cornishman, which has never been beaten yet in the West of England, and which makes its first a p p sera o ce this year at the Royal show. Mr. Baker's Ball, which gets third priz.?, has great substance, and won second prize at the Eeses County ehow.. Grand Ruth scarcely received his due on the pre- sent occasion, his length of quarters and u b- stance seeming to warrant a higher place. The class for bulls calved in 1882 is not a large one. Mr, Thompson's Royal Baron, which heads it, is a fine roan. and Mr. Coomer's Sir Stafford, which gets ercond prize, is very compact and level, though a much smaller animal than the other. The bulls calved in 1883 were headed, as they have been at ihveral previous shows, by Mr. William Handley's Royal Ingram, Mr. Rudsdale's Lord Salisbury coming in second, a equare-bailt, thickly-fleshed' animal, ' which took a first prize of £5O at the Birmingham spring sale in March last, and is very compact, although not quite of the nice character of his leading competitor, which dis- plays more uniform depth and substance, Messrs. Ho;ken and Son's Duke of Ilayles 60h, and Mr. Foljambe's Prince, displayed well in the ring: The youngest bull class is, as usual, a very large one, and has is it many promising ani- mals. Ile Duke of Northumberland's Hopewell, which heads it, is exceeding broad and level over the back, and altogether is a remarkably fine animal for his age. Mr. Handley's Golden Treasure is a well.known son of Sir Arthur Ingram, of which a description need not be given. The third prize is won by the Duke of Devonshire's Baron Oxford 18th, lengthy in quarters, with good ribs, and very robust and promising. The Duke of Northumberland's two cows, which take first and second prizes, may be con,idered good model shorthorns, and Rosalind .12th has a handsome bead. She is quite worthy of her position. THURSDAY.—V.DeIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES. The Prince of Wales left Studley, the seat of the Marquis

ef Ripon, on Thursday morning fer Presten to visit the Royal Agritaltural Show and inaugurate the new docks. His Royal Highness was attended by Mr. Tyrwhitt Wilson, and travelled quite privately. A special London and North- Western frain was placed at his disposal, and passed the junction at Leeds shortly after eleven, being timed to reach Presten at one. The Princeu of Wales returned to London the same day. Rain fell heavily during Wednesday night, and the decora- tions which have been effected in honour of the Royal via have suffered considerably therefrom. The weather continued tolerably fine en Thursday morning, despite the heavy banks of threataning clouds, and thousands of people polared into the borough from the surrounding towns and villages. The streets were almost impassable, and his Royal Highness had a true Lancashire welcome. The Prince arrived at the Central Station shortly before one, and was received by the Mayor and Corporation in their official capacity. Lords Sefton and Latham were also present. En route for the Corn Exchange, where a loyal address was presented by the Mayor, a large crowd had assembled, also along the route to the show yard, and the Cheering was enthusiastic and continuous the whole dis- tance to Moor Park. The Prince has been elected for the third time President of the Society. On arriving at Moor Park. the Prince was received by Sir Massey Lopes, M.P., President, on behalf of the Ctaincil of the Society, and hav- ing been presented with his badge as Trustee and President- elect of the Society, he was conducted by Mr. Jacob Wilson to the members' large tent, where the general meeting was about to commence. Subsequently, his Royal Highness lunched privately with the stewards, and witnessed the parade of horses. A general meeting of the members of the society, Presi- ded over by the Prince of Wales, who took his seat as pre- sident for the ensuing year, was held in the large tent near the centre of the groand.—At half-past three a grand parade of agricultural and cart horses, followed by a parade of thoroughbreds, hunters, hackneys, and ponies took place in the presence of the Prince of Wales and a distinguished company, who viewed the spectacle from a red-draperied balcony. A little after five the Prince left the show ground for the Preston station, whence he departed for Ormakirk en route to Latham House, where he stays for the night.—Tbe general exhibition of implements at rest and in motion was continued throughout the day. The weather has been fair but cold, a strong wind blowing from the north-west. The attendance on Thurs- day was far in excess of the two previous ones, and the local gentry and tradespeople patronised the show in a very encouraging madner. The annual meeting of the Short- horn Society was held in the members' tent in the morning, Mr. M. El. IV. Beauford, president, occupyingthe chair. The report of the council wee adopted unanimously. The society's funds amount to £3,313 18s id, principally in- vested in Consols. The retiring officers were re-elected, and also the retiring members of the council. The Earl of Bective moved, and Mr. S. B. Foster seconded, a vote of thanks to the president, which was carried non. con. It will be remembered that at the meeting held in December last, at the Royal Agricultural Hall, the society decided to offer for competition at the Preston meeting two prizes of £25 each, one for the best male shorthorn, and one for the best female shorthorn. Up to five o'clock in the afternoon the attendance was officially registered at 21.583.

CAIRO, SATIIRDAY.—GeneraI Brackenbury telegraphed yesterday from Fatrneh, announcing receipt of a letter from a merchant at Ilindak, dated °Lb inst., stating that the Mandi was dead, and that his followers were fighting among themselves. In a second telegram despatched to-day,General Brackenbury reports the arrival at Fatmeh yesterday of a refugee Egyptian soldier, who states that he saw at Abudom on the Ist inst., an Arab from Khartoum who confirmed the news of the Mandi's death.

Paws, SUNDAY.—The Intransigeant publishes a letter from M. Billing, stating that the Matadi, previous to the capture of Khartoum, offered to send General Gordon to the English advanced posts in consideration of a ransom of 1250,000 f., to be paid by Lord Lyons directly the official news of the surrender of Gordon reached Paris. M. Billing forwarded this proposal to Lord Lyons, bat it was rejected by the British Government. ALEXANDRIA, MONDAY.—A telegram was received this morning from Father Bonomi, who states that Oliver Paine died after a severe illness at Omdurman. No official con- firmation has yet been received of the Mandi's death. 4.lmiceNDllLt, TIIIIDADAY.—Tbe Egyptian, Gazette states that among the better class of the hiusenlonn poplalation in Lower hgypt it is believed that the blandi died previous to the departure of Hussein Pasha Khalifa, who would not otherwise have been allowed to leave the Soudan. FIRE IN RUSSIA.—FIFTY ROUSE., BURNED DOWN.

Si. PETERSBURG, BUNDAL—A great fire broke out yes- terday at Kursk, and more than fifty houses in the cemmer- cial quarter of the town were destroyed. The loses are very great. THE FRENCH IN ANNA.—THE KIN.I A PRISONER. '

• PARIS, SATURDAY.—Fresh treasure has been found in the Palace at Hue. The Z,uaves have the custody of the silver bars and other treasure to the value of ten million francs. General de Conroy says the King of Annam is at a place to the rear of Camil. a prisoner of the Insurgent Thuyet, and that the Queen Mother, the King's uncles, the Princes of the Royal family, and a number of Mandarins have intimated their wish to return to Hue. PARIS, TITURSDAY.—The Minister of War has received the following telegram from General de Conroy, dated Hue, yesterday, 11 am.:—" Happy to inform you that all the Princes of the blood have returned here, and are now assem- bled at the French Legation. Thoaman, uncle of King Tu Duc, has been designated by the Royal Family as sole Regent until the King's return. The Princes will take up their residence on their estates. The Queen mother returns to-morrow with the King's wives, and will reside in the palace attached to the Tu Due Mausoleum." FRENCH TROUBLES IN SENEGAL.

Pause, SATURDAY—The Government have received a despatch from the Governor of Senegal, dated July 9th, describing the state of affairs on the Upper Senegal river. The Governor says :—" Although there is nothing disquiet- ing in the present situation, information has been received that the Chief Samory attacked Capt. Louvel on 3%1 ey 31st between Niagassola and Tiguire. Commander Combes went to Captain ILouvel's assistance, forcing the passages of the river held by the blacks, upon whom he inflicted a severe check. On June 6th Commander Combes again encountered and defeated the rebels at Sicatoca, where he had gone to .revictual his troops, leaving sixty men with provisions at Niagassola. Having collected ample supplies of provisions and ammunition, he returned to Niagasaola with the inten• ton of finally diepersing the rebels under Samory." OUTBREAK OF TYPHUS_ AMONG FRENCH

Pants, SATURDLY.—Telegrams from Marseilles state that the sanitary condition of the military camp at Pas des Landers is becoming worse, and that owing to the numerous cases of typhus among the troops, the immediate dissolution of the camp is regarded as imperative. MADRID, SATURD&Y.—A serious riot occurred yesterday at Lerida against the new Excise law. The mob seized and burnt the Excise Collector's box. The military were called out and dispersed the rioters. Several shots were fired, and a number of persons were killed and wounded, the former includinz one officer and four soldiers. REPUBLICAN CONSPIRACY IN SPAIN.
MADRID, TLIDRSDAY.—SeveraI arrests have been made at Saragossa in connection with a conspiracy for a Repub- lican rising, the existence of which is suspected by the au- th critics.

WASETINGTON, SATURDAY.—Nfr. Endicott, secretary for War, has ordered 3,000 troops under the command of General Sheridan to proceed immediately to Fort Reno, in the In- dian territory. It is reported from Colorado City, Texas, that a battle has been fought between the cowboys and Indians in New Mexico. Sixty Indians and 16 cowboys are stated to have been killed in the en.zagernent. WASHINGTON', MONDAY.—Tbe Colombian Minister here has received intelligence stating that the Colombian rebels at Barrangailla, persisting in their 'determination to go up the Mag,dalena river, have been completely routed at Cali- mar. Their fleet W3S damaged by an explosion which oc- curred on hoard the boat conveying the ammunition. Almost all the revolutionary leaders are believed to have perished.

Mils; WEDNESDAY.—Oa the occasion of the Frsnch national fete M. Cambon held a receception yesterday of the French colony. The Resident Geaeral delivered a speech, in the courao of which he dwelt upon the benefits which s French protectorate conferred upon Tunis, whose finances now were in a prosporons condition. FAMINE IN KORDOFAN. CAIRO, WEDNESDay.—The report of the Mandi's death is generally believed be the Arabs of the tipper class in this city. Hussein l'as'na Khalfa states that Lupton Bey and the garrison under his command have arrived at Sea- naar. The famine in Kordofan is assuminv terrible proportions, and in Khartoum there is great searcity of food. The rebela are not expected to advance towards Dongola for several months yet.

1 RUSSIA AND AFGHANISTAN. TEHERAN, WEDNESDAY.—Considerabla Russian rein- forcements have arrived at Mery and Pul-i-Khisti during the last fortnight. Four regiments of Afghan infantry from Cabal have reached Herat, and four others are on their way thither front the Haztra district. JARDORAHATEN (VIA MESHED), JULY 11.--It Is rumoured that the Russians have advanced in force to Zulficar. They are treating the Persian territory as though it were Russian. The Frontier Mission is about to move to the vicinity of Herat, whither the engineer officers have already gone. Reinforcements are arriving at Askabad. ' The Afghans are anxiona but resolute. They are puzzled by these warlike preparations under cover of pacific assurances. It is be- lieved that Colonel tlikhanoff has determined to force on a war, and is deceiving the Czar.—Times. Simla, THIIRSDAY.—Captain Tate and Captain Peacock have arrived at Herat, in compliance with the request of the Afghan officials, in order to inspect the fortifications of the place. The other members of the Boundary Commis- sion have moved forward in the direction of Herat, with the object of placing themselves within easy reach of communi- cation. The Central News understands that, although no official Information has yet been received confirming the reported advance in force upon Zulificar by the Russians, reports have reached the British authorities from various quarters, all tending to give some pro'tability to the rumours now in circulation. On the Stock Exchange a better feeling pre- veiled in consequence of the absence of definite information one way or another. Consols therefore improved an eighth, and Russians a half to one.

div.head: WELSH BREACH OF PROMISE.
div.p: A WELSH BREACH OF PROMISE.

Mr. Justice Cave and a special jury were engaged at Monmouth Assizes, on Thursday. in hearing a breach of promise action brought by Louisa Bailey, daughter of the supervising engineer at Merthyr Vale Colliery, Glamorgan- shire, against Morgan Davis Llewellyn, mining engineer, of Pontypool. The claim was for £3,000. The plaintiff left home bee iuse her father married again, and while engaged at a millinery establishment at Pontypool, and at Christ- mail, 1882, she made the defendant's acquaintance in a rail- way carriage. They afterwards became engaged, and at the defendant's instigation, on leaving the situation, she went to Haverfordwest College to improve her education and learn classics and music; and also the less showy but important art of cooking. Whilst at the college the defen- dant became cool, and told her in his letters that he prefer- red a bachelor's life, and ultimately the affair was broken Off. After an interval of five or six months the parties again met in a railway compartment. A reconciliation took place, and the defendant promised to marry her when two Chancery suits whic a he had against his mother and sisters were settled. The defendant afterwards made an excuse about an anonymous letter which contained reference to one of the members of the plaintiff's family, and declined to carry out the promise, pretending that he was making inquiries to ascertain whether she was a suitable person to marry. He also said his mother was opposed to the match, and that, as Mr. Jelf said, his sisters, and aunts, and cousins would de- cline to recognise him if he married a poor milliner's assis- tant. The peculiarity of the long correspondence was that there was no solitary term of endearment or affection. They I commenced "Dear Miss Bailey," and ended "Yours sin- cerely "or " Yours very sincerely." This was owing to the defendant's excessive prudence. The defendant was shown to be of good family, with :caw a year, besides hav- ing private means. The defence was that the promise of marriage was strictly conditional and contingent, but the defendant made a poor figure in the witness box, owing partly to a lack of fluency in speaking English. When pressed he took refuge, amidst convulsions of laughter, be- hind a large diary, which he produced to prove what he did on certain occasions. He admitted baying purchased a ring for another young lady.—The jury found for the plaintiff, damages £1,200. The judge stayed execution for a week.
LAND LAW REFOOL-LKTTER FROM
JOHN BRIGHT.

The folio wing correspondence has been made public : Kensington Park Gardens, W., July 6, 1855. Dear Mr. Bright,—The time is ripe for promoting practieal measures of land law reform, and for urging such measures upon the attention of those who will have to 'elect the next House of Commons. For the interested consideration of such pro- posals the present circumstances of agriculture are ex- tremely favourable With the intention of renewing such efforts as I have made in that direction, I wish to ask your opinion of the following programme. I believe it would es- tablish that policy of" free land "of which you were one of the earliest advocates :—(1) Abolition of the law of primogeniture; (2) abolition of copyhold and customary tenure ; (3) prohibition of settlement of land upon unborn persons, and of the general power of creating life estates in land ; (4) conveyance by registration of title ; all interests in the property registered to be recorded ; (5) provision for the sale of encumbered settled property. Our present laws encourage separation of ownership from occupation of land. That tendency is not in harmony with the general interests of the people. The position of the occupier de- mands fuller security, such at least as Sir James Caird sug- gested by way of amendment of the Agricultural Holdings Act, in order to secure the sitting tenant against liability to lose his share of increased letting value consequent upon his improvements, by a rise of rent or by exaction of an unfair rent, to which he can offer no resistance except bv notice to quit, involving serious depreciation of his stock in trade. The extension in principle, and under proper safeguards, of , the purchase clauses of the Irish Land Acts to Great Britain I and the enfranchisement of leaseholds are practical matters which should be admitted to full and fair consideration. More than 2,000,000 acres of the best land are held by cor- porations in mortmain. This tenure involves serious evils, I iacluding absentee ownership in perpetuity and a most un- just exemption from taxation. I have met with *so exposi- tion of this policy more concise and acceptable than is con- ' tained in your own words :—" We would so change our laws as to give to every present generation an absolute control over the soil, free from the paralysing influences which , afflict it now from the ignorance, the folly, the obstinacy, or the pride of the generations which have passed away."— Yours very sincerely, ARTHUR ARNOLD.—The Right Hon. John Bright, M.P. 132, Piccadilly, W., July 9, 1885.—Dear Mr. Arnold,—l have received with much pleasure your letter of the 6th instant, and have read with much interest your suggestions on the reform of our land laws—the great question which will demand, and I hops receive, the attention of the Par- liament which will be elected in November next. I look back with intense satisfaction on the reform of our tariff, begun by Sir Robert Peel in the year 1842, carried forward by him in the year 1846, when the odious Cora Law was condemned and abolished, and completed in after years by the great measures carried through Parliament by Mr. Glad- stone. In connection with the changes in our commercial policy, the names of Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Gladstone will for ever stand foremost and highest in the list of the Ministers and statesmen of our country. They have lifted to a higher scale of independence and comfort the indstse Wong millions of our people. My lamented friend Mr. Cobden, who did not underrate the result of the strpggle in which he had taken so eminent a part, on more than one occasion expressed the belief that the men or the Minister who should hereafter free the land of the United Kingdom from the fetters which have hitherto bound it would confer as great a blessing on our people as that bestowed upon them by the freedom of the produce of the soil. The time has now come when this new great land question must be discussed and settled. lt is well that some plans, just to the nation, and not less just to the pos- sessors ef land, should be brought before the attention of our people. In the suggestions which you have submitted to me you offer such a plan, and! cannot but hope that it will receive, as I believe it will deserve, a very large measure of support throughout the country. There have been wild schemes brought before some portions of our people, schemes not bisod on any just principle; your auggestions seemed to me just and calculated to do good to landowner, to ten- nant farmer, to the industrious labourer of the soil, and to the millions whose families subsist upon its produce. I cannot enter into anything like a great movement in con- nection with this question, but I hope we may soon see a movement in thi.; constituencies and in Parliament, and that anothsr great measure of reform may soon be added to those 'ay which our time and our generation are already dis- tinguished. Believe me, very sincerely yours. JOHN BRlGHT.—Arthur Arnold, Esq., M.P., 45, Kensington Park Gardens.

The Queen has commissioned Mr. it. Caton Wood- ville to furnisk a painting of the forthcoming royal wed- ding. &THINE IN THE COTTON TRADE—The Council of the Oldham Operative Spinners' Association have fiaally decided to re- commend a general strike against the reduction in wages of 10 per cent proposed by the masters. It is expected that about 30,000 co!ton operatives will immediately "come out " for an indefinite period. The association has issued a circular ID its members asking for support in the crisis. MILITARY DISTURBANCES.—A MAN KILLED.—At Water. ford, on Monday, an inquest was held on the body of John Grant, who was bayonetted on Sunday by a PrivAle of the Ist South Wales Borderers during a disturtk.nce between soldiers and civilians. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was wilfully stabbed by a soldier of the regiment named, and that, in the interests of the peace of the city, the regiment should be removed to some other station. AYLESBURY ExEcTroar. The polling at Aylesbury for the election of a Parliamentary representative to fill the vacancy caused by the elevation of Sir Nathaniel k(oths- child, Liberal, to the peerage, opened at eight o'clock on Thursday morning. The candidates were Mr. William Graham, Conservative, and Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild, Liberal. The result of the poll was as follows : Rothschild (L), 2,353; Graham ‘C), 1,416; Liberal majority, 937. THE MURDER AND SUICIDE IN WALES.—The District Coroner, on Thursday, held an inquest on the body of Elizibetii Bees and her child, who were found drowned at Dowlsis, Rhondda Valley. It was alleged that the unfor- tunate woman had been most cruelly treated by her hus- band. A verdict of "Wilful murder " was returned against the dead woman in the case of the child, and of " Suicide " in her own case. The Coroner severely cen- sured the husband for his cruel conduct, which, he believed, had led to the sad tragedy, and he regretted that ,the law did not reach such cases. 1 ONE CASE of Army cud Navy hi FDICENE3 contains sotTi dent to cure contagious diseases of a certain class (internal r external); ,ts. 6d., parcels post ss. div.head: NEW BOOKS &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS &c.

"The Poetical Works of Robert Buahanan " are issued by Messrs. Chatto and Windns in a popular edition of one volume. The book is fittingly, that is to say, handsomely presented, and it is adornad with a very fine portrait of the author with facsimile auto- graph. We are glad to think that, laid before the public in this form, the poet is likely to become better known to the masses, for hitherto it has been beyond the reach of the ordinary reader to obtain a complete set of his works. Poets, like other craftsmen, require feeding and clothing, and therefore to be paid for their labour. No one who could afford to pay would ever begrudge Mr. Buchanan the price of his varions works as they were issued ; but now they are brought together in one volume they will reach and gratify the million, and at the same time prove, we trust, • profitable to the author. It is getting on for a score • of years since Robert Buchanan first began to charm the English ear as a singer of sweet songs; and the world has something to be thankful for that he has increased in power and sweetness as he has increased in years. Undoubtedly in his early poems he revealed traces of the influence of other writers. What author of note has not shown himself susceptible to similar impressions? But it was soon seen that he did not require any outside aid—that be was a true poet— "native and to the manner born " ; and every year adds to the host of his admirers. There are few writers who ean touch the pathetic side of life 80 powerfully and yet 80 delicately • he goes straight to the heart, and yet he is never tricky or vulgar. There is nothing in the whole range of English literature finer in its way than " Lord Ronald's Wife." How forcible and how original the simile— .

And saw the damp chill dawn stare in Like a dim drown'd face with oozy eyes. But the poet abounds in unforgettable lines which are likely to become "household words." Glancing through the first few pages of the volume, and not- ing some that we have marked we come across— The waggons rumbling in the rutted lanes. Sound and sense are here wedded in such a way that they cannot be divorced. Then we have a passage descriptive of the stillness before the storm— The wind dies—not a leaf stirs—on the pool The fly scarce moves ; Earth seems to hold her breath Until her heart stops, listening silently For the far footstep of the coming rain Again— The air is hotter here; the bee booms by With hemp-laden thigh, Doubling the heat with sounds akin to heat. And what more charming—fragrant let us say than— And yonder, dark with dreaming of the rare, Grows the wood-violet like a lowly thought. Buchanan, conscious of his strength, seems to have been careless of using phrases which left him open to plagiarism. Tennyson in " Lockaley Hall" speaks of being "upon the hills like gods together careless of mankind " ; and in Bachanan's " Cloudland "we have--
Oh is it not sweet, sweet, sweet, To be in this green retreat, In a beautiful half-dream, Like a god on a hill. In his "To David in Heaven" there occur the lines—
Higher yet and higher, Ever nigher, ever nigher, while in Shelley's " Ode to a Skylark" we have— Higher still and higher . .

From the earth thou springest. Many other suggestive passages might be put side by side; but we are not disposed to endeavour to make it out that our song-bird depends for his beauty on borrowed plumes; it is too late in the day for such a charge to be sustained. Buchanan is a poet of the first rank; he is a poet too of the people; he sings their loves, and joys, and sorrows--" the pathos and the power of common life "—and we commend his works to the masses—a stout volume of over 500 double-column pages—well persuaded that those who spend their silver upon and dip into his book will find that they have invested in a mine of gold. "Better than Revenge" is the title of a story by a local author, Mr. C. A. Luffman, of Newton-le- Willows. It is exceedingly well written, while the simplicity of treatment is charming. The characters, though not numerous, are well drawn; and they are all of a kind to interest the reader. Mr. Luff man must be congratulated on his success, and we trust his shilling novel will have a large sale. Mr. John Heywood, Manchester and London, is the publisher. Cassell's "Etiquette of Good Society" has reached the forty-second thousand, and we do not marvel at its popularity. It is a cheap, handy, and handsome volume; and the various topics are dealt with in a practical and attractive style. Everything is treated of—birth, marriage, and death, and the hundred and one social observances that come between. Reference to particular points is easy, as there is a copious index.

The July part of "Little Folks" commences a new volume. There is a beautiful coloured plate as frontispiece, entitled "Great Expectations," while the rest of the illustrations leave nothing to be desired. Verse, stories, and sketches are of a kind to please big as well as little folks. There is a special list of prizes announced, open to home, foreign, and colonial competition—that is to readers resident in all parts of the world. "Bright Days" is the title of the holiday number of Cassell's Magazine. It is a charming number— just the thing for the seaside or country. The articles are of most varied kind; there is an excellent prize gavotte for violin and pianoforte, by Mr. W. W. Pearson ; and there are severel capital short stories. " Caesell's Magazine" for July is also strong; the frontispiece alone is worth the price of the magazine. "The Quiver" leads off with an article "The Rolls call of the Heroes," which is deeply interesting. Cassell. s "Magazine of Art" for July opens with a smart "New Song of Spring Gardens' by ; Mr. A. Dobson, and it is cleverly illustrated by Mr. R. Caldecott. The fine engravings of "The Olden , London Churches " show that the Metropolis has I features of interest which are too often overlooked. I "On the Appian Way," from the picture by Gabriel Max, is a striking piece of work which does justice to the original. The river Dart has many admirers, and their number will be largely increased by the cheering pictures,of it in this issue. The full page reproduo- tion of "A Cry from the Deep" will be sure to catch the eyes of those who are on the look out for good subjects for framing. "The Return from School" is a delicate facsimile ; it well repays the most careful examination. "The Modern Medallions" are very vigorous ; but that of Victor Hugo is per- haps the least successful. We have also to hand the current issues of Cassell's Popular Gardening, Book of Health, Recent British Battles, the Eneyclopmdic Dictionary, and the fine art edition of Longfellow. • An excellent brochure, entitled " Hints on English Composition," has just been issued by Mr. J. Keefe, F.R U.S., &e., of Liverpool. Though confined to seven octavo pages and in pamphlet form, the little work contains many aids to good prose composition. The essential points of grammar and style are con- cisely yet clearly treated, and by way of models, two outline essays are given for imitation. The sugges- tions are just those a civil service candidate will appreciate. Messrs. Jerrold and Sons, London, the publishers of what is known as the " Gdes's Trip series, have just added " Daisy Dimple ; her loves and her lovers." The sketches are in the Norfolk dialect, and there is some racy reading in them. Politics in the mouth of " Daisy "are a little out of place, but as the writer has a hit at both sides, and does not make politics a feature, he will be pardoned. "The Little One's Own Coloured Picture Paper," edited by Mrs. E. Day, maintains the good start it made. Stories an:, pictures are alike good, and the paper is sure to become a f avcurite with the little ones. A Practicable Decimal System for Great Britain and her Colonies" is the title of a valuable pamphlet by Mr. R. T. Rohde. Ir. advocat,s a much-needed reform, and removes much misoonception on the sub- ject. "The Season" and " Le Moniteur dc la Mode " for Jul' are charming as ever as fashion journals, with their coloured plitps, paper natt.erns, and numberless illustrations. " Myra s Journal" and " Myra's Threepenny Journal," also to hand, are equally good in their way, the difference in price being taken into account.

ENCOTMOING THE GROWTH OF POPLHATION. France is making a determined effart to quicken the slow rate at which her population has lately been growing. Tne Cham- ber has just voted a grant of 400.000 francs to provide, at the public expense, for the education and board of every eeventh child born in a French f.nally. A family with two children—and this is what most French couples allow them- selves—will think with despair on the. amount crf lee-way to be made up before the seventh child is born. The hardest case of all will be where the effort is made and is followed with only partial success. The country will be the gainer. Out of six children there will be more material for the army and for the colonies than out of two. Bat for six children there is no reward promised. and the eight francs will be unearned as long as the seventh is still maborn !

div.head: SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON
div.p: SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON

BA.RRAOKS. - 7 Denis O'Leary, Quartermaster-Sergeant in the 3rd Battalion (King's) Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, Warrington, shot himself through the head with a rifle on 'Monday morning in it tragic manner. A. comrade found his body in the back store-room, lying upon some clothing, with a recently discharged rifle on the ground near by. To the trig- ger of the rifle was attached a piece of string, done up in a loop, and appearances led to the conclusion that detteased, whose shoes and stockings were of, placed the muzzle of the vveapon—a Martini-Henri— to his mouth, aud exploded it by putting the toe of his right foot through the loop and thus pulling the trigger. The bullet passed out at the back of his head and indented the opposite wall, from which it rebounded and was lost. Deceased was 45 years of age, was married and had four children, and had seen about twenty six years' army service, a noitioa of the time having been spent in India. He was liked and esteemed by his comrades in arms, and his tragic death is greatly deplored- He is spoken of as having been a man of very temperate habits, but of late he had been somewhat despondent, and his mind was evidently unhinged. On the discovery of the death information was given to the police, who com- municated with the Coroner, and on Tuesday after- noon Mr. Brighouse and a jury attended at the Bar. racks, where an inquiry was held at the hospital.— Col.-Sergeant William Spendilow 3rd Battalion laver- pool Regiment, deposed that he knew deceased vtaal. Deceased was quartermaster-sergeant in the same regiment, and was about 45 years of age. Witnees had known him inearly five years, and last saw him alive la.tween seven and eight o'clock on Monday motlaing. Witness was then at his house, 201, Or and deceased passed. Witness called out. "Good morning, Quarter,, ' but deceased did not then take any notice. Witness called out in a louder tone, and deceased then came to him. Witness asked him what had been the matter with him lately, and if money matters were troubling him. Deceased said, " Nonsense ; it was nothing," but he seemed nearly "full up," and as though he were going to cry. Witness added that if deceased was in want of money he knew where to get it. Deceased said, " Oh, no," and walked away, his head down, as though he were in deep trouble. About 10-45 witness went to the store-room to draw boots for recruits from deceased, who, however, was not there, The door of the bank store-room was slightly ajar, and witness called out, " Denis, are you there ?' Net receiving an answer, he went into the room, and saw deceased lying as though asleep on his back, on two bales of elo,hing. Witness saw that the bales were covered with blood, and that O'Leary was dead, He ran and told Quartermaster-Sergeant Brown and reported the matter at the orderly-room. A rifi ifrom.that had been exploded was near the body. There was a string tied round the trigger and the shoes acd stockings of deceased were off. The stringe the trigger, round the trigger guard, and up to the. cleaning rod. An examination of the body allowed that a bullet must have gone through the bank of do- ceased's neck. The course of the ballot indicated that deceased was in a reclining posture when he die- charged the gun. Deceased had been despondent and aosentsminned for the last two or three Weeks.: He was a steady, respectable man, beloved by everyone in the barraeirs.—Sergeant-Major William Burns, erd Battalion Liverpool Reaiment, said that he also had known deceased for five years. He gave evi- dence regarding the finding of the body, and said that at the end of the string attached to the trigger was a loop. There was no doubt deceased exploded the rifle with the right toe. The ballet passed I through the head and came out in a line with the right ear at the back of the head. It then struck the wall opposite and made an indentation. Deceased had been despondent for tiblut four months.— Quartermaster-Sergeant George Brown 4th Battalion Liverpool Regiment, who gave evidence, thought de- ceased had seemed strange since January, Dsait had given up his pension and re-joined, thinking would benefit him, but he seemed to have been troubled about it, and to think that he had made a mistake.—The Coroner having summed up, the jury returned a verdict to the efit that deceased shot himself when temporarily insane. The remains of Quartermaster. Sergeant Denis O'Leary were on Wednesday afternoon interred wek military honours at Warrington cemetery. The funeral was. at tended by a large number of the mili- tary stationed at Orford barraeks, and the ceremony was also witnessed by many civilians, deceased hav- ing been well-known and esteemed. There were two- military bands, and the firing party fired throe volleys over the grave.
