scorrs BILIOUS AND LIVER PILLS families--acting on the first impulse—ceased PIitPARED WII ROUT MERCURY. AN EFNEM ['ITU, REMEDY to subscribe to the paper and wrote strong FOR ALL LIVER COMPLAINTS. I letters of complaint to the Editor. But the

question still remained—Are these things true, or are they not true? Here is a report of a careful and prolonged investigation which tells us of procurers who are regularly engaged in the traffic of supplying vergins of tender years in order that titled ° and other scoundrels (princes and legislators included) may steep themselves in sensuality without risk of the punishment which sometimes fol- lows on vicious indulgence ;tells of lambs led to the slaughter in utter ignorance of what they are doing and whither they are going ; of debased mothers who sell their children to a slavery wore than death and of school children lured away from their homes by fiendish women who track them down to hand them over to brutal men. We cannot ignore this story of" hell's contagion breath- ing on the world ;" and we are glad to know that its truth is to be sifted to the bottom. Four good men and true—Mr. SAMUEL MORLEY, CARDINAL MANNING, the BisHoP; of LONDON. and the ARCHBISHOP of CANTER- BURY—have accepted the invitation of the Editor of the "Pall Mall Gazette" to con- stttute themselves a court of investiga- tion. They are pledged to secrecy as to persons and places, for the evid- ence which has been obtained has for the most part been obtained on the understanding that it shall not be used for the purpose of a prosecution or for exposure. They will make a report, and it will then be known whether the " Gazette " has in any respect exaggerated or " set down aught in malice." Meantime good is arising out of evil; the pressure of public opinion is already such that there is no fear that the Criminal Law Amendment Bill which is before Parlia- ment will not be passed with what is known as "the age of consent" raised. As the law stands, a girl of fourteen is regarded as hav- ing arrived at the years of maturity and dis- cretion. This is absurd and must be altered. As Professor STUART said the other night, a girl is unable to buy a glass of beer till she is sixteen, and yet she is assumed to have arrived at a competent age at fourteen to decide as to selling her own virtue! On Tuesday night there was a large meeting in London at which this question was con- sidered, and a resolution was passed suggest- ing that the age should be altered to 18 years. It was also resolved that provision should be made for the effective punishment of pro- curation of seduction, and that there be an " increase of the safeguards against the de- coying of innocent and the detention of un- willing girls for immoral purposes." Mrs. BOOTH, who spoke with great feeling at this gathering, said she had received a letter from the QUEEN, and " her MAJESTY'S heart, thank God ! beat in the right place on this question." This is well ; it will be a warning, let us hope, to the debauchees amongst the aristocracy, who, for obvious reasons, are at the present moment decrying the investiga- tion which they fear. This is essentially a question for the people ; it is the children of the poor who are made the victims of the rich. We have heard much, at times, of the degradatioh of the masses; but their conduct is angelic compared with that of the butchers in high places, who would seize the innocent and destroy them, body and soul. Too 10w,.b have these monsters been permitted to pol- lute the land; but a cry—a bitter cry—is going up against them the day of reckoning is at hand.

Tna Orangemen of Warrington had a day out on Saturday; they went to Culcheth and had dinner, and the fresh air had such an effect upon them that speeches were made which were curious even for Orangemen. Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, who will talk about Sir GIL- BERT GREENALL, and who will say things that he shouldn't say, went out of his way to tell the audience that the Brewer of Wilders- pool "had represented them for a quar.er of a century in Parliament, and during that time he had never once promised them one thing that he had not carried out." Unfortunately, he did not go on to say what it was that Sir GILBERT had promised, and what he had done. We do know that he voted against working-men living in the country having the franchise conferred upon them ; and he showed his further regard for working-men who happen to be soldiers by voting not only against the abolition of flogging in the army, but against a reduction even in the number of lashes. Are these what are reckoned amongst his promises and performances? If so, the " disgrace " would be to return such a representative at the next election. Mr. W. DICKENS, harping on the same string, said he "desired that they should return Sir GILBERT to Parliament without having to resort to bribery and corruption. The bribery and corruption at the last elec- tion was something beyond description, and would have unseated any member." Mr. DICKENS no doubt knows, for it is out of the fulness of the heart that the mouth speaketh. He is penitent "beyond description "in view of the fact that the late Liberal Government passed an act which makes it dangerous to resort to the old-fashioned Tory malprac- tices. It is his desire that they shouldn't have to "resort to bribery and corruption ;" and he appeals to them to think of the con- sequences. He knows something of the old Adam there is in them, and he is obviously afraid that what is bred in the bone will not be got out of the flesh. The Rev. J. M. SANGAR, who has recently come to Warring- ton, expressed himself as "taken by sur- prise " in being called upon to respond to the toast of "The Protestant Bishops and Clergy throughout England." We cannot but think that, in turn, his audience would be "taken by surprise" at his speech. He began by stating that he had "the greatest respect for all the bishops and clergy of the Church of England," and ended by saying "they knew that certain Bishops and clergymen had falsified their oath of allegiance, and had de- liberately aided in those things which they , had sworn to drive away. This was really the case with some of the Bishops conse- crated a few years ago. It was true at their consecration they consented to support Pro- testantism, but subsequently they had done their utmost to uproot it, and he trembled for , the future of the English Church." We must confess to feeling somewhat bewildered at this speech ; it is " more exquisite than the other." How can even an Orange Chaplain respect men who have "falsified their oath of allegiance ?" How can he respect that which is not in itself respectable ? Surely Orange- men have some regard for "the eternal verities." For our own part, we have no res- pect for men—bishops though they be—who do not keep their word, to say nothing about falsifying an oath of allegiance. Our Orange friends have not done themselves justice at Culcheth ' • the fresh air seems to have been too much for them; and we trust they are all right again now that they are back to smoke- smitten Warrington.

SIR RICHARD CROSS, replying to a ques- tion in the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening, said the Government, after giving the matter careful consideration, had come to the conclusion not to prosecute the Editor of the "Pall Mall Gazette" in respect of certain articles published last week which were alleged to constitute an obscene publication. People in the provinces who are not readers Of the " Gazette " have been wondering what the Editor of that journal has been doing to get himself in such questionable repute. It Would seem that he has by "the skin of his teeth," as it were, escaped being " run in" for !nthlishing indecent literature; but those who take this view should know that the gentle- na, an in question has had no fear of the law before his eyes. On the contrary, he has in- Vited—we may say clamoured for a prosecu- tli;°n, denouncing the attack upon small boys for selling the paper as a cowardly pro- eeeding, seeing that he held himself fully responsible for what he had written and Published. JOHN BRIGGS, OF W7I,NES. Mr. John Briggs, the Lancashi,e county professional cricketer, who is rapidly rising to fame, was married on Tuesday to Miss Alice Burgess. The ceremony took place at Finn- worth Parish Church, but the event had been Ipt so secret that although the bridegroom is very popular in Widnes, only a few persons were preSent in the stcred edifice. Messrs. Pilling, Barlow, and Watson, well-known profes- sionals, officiated as groomsmen. The service was peformed by the Rev. George Bond. After partaking of breakfast at the house of the bridegroom's father, the newly-married Couple departed to Manchester where they intend take up their residence until the conclusion of the cricketing season.

THE Liberals of the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire, if they have been a little behind as to time in selecting a candi- date, are not at all behind in the kind of man they have secured to fight the battle for them. In Mr. E. K. MusrAArr, J.P., they have a candidate who, if elected, will be a credit to the constituency and to the House of Com- mons. In another column we give a sketch of his career, from which it will be seen that he is admirably fitted by natural endowment and past training to become a legislator He has an excellent record, and we judge of the tree by its fruits. He is not a hanger-on of commerce or of politics, but one who, though still in the prime of life, has for a generation done yeoman service. Whilst studying chemistry in Germany many years ago, Mr. MUSPRATT became impressed with the fact that England was behind her continental neighbours in educational matters; hence the deep interest he has since taken in encouraging science and art classes in this country. He may be said to be of the school, in politics, of JOHN STUART MILL, de- manding that a problem shall be thought out, and that sound principle shall be the basis of action. He has long and consistently advocated reform in our system, of taxation. and is now the president of that invaludole institution-the Financial Reform Association. He is a member, too, of the Liverpool Cham- ber of Commerce, and, as chairman of the Home Trade and Railway Committee in con- nection with that body, he possesses a mine of information which would be of great ser- vice in the discussion of commercial questions in the House of Commons. Mr. MUSPRATT enjoys a high reputation, as a manufacturer ' amongst those who are engaged in the alkdi trade, and has been elctecli President of the Society of Chemical Industry for the Present year. He is the right sort of man to send to the new Parliament, and we trust the Liberals of the Widnes Division will do him and themselves justice by working hard and heartily to ensure his being returned to St. Stephen's.

ST...IOHN THE EVANGELIST'S? WEsrow.—The anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday, in the afternoon by the Rev. T. M. Urmson, of Runcorn, and in the evening by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, incumbent of Weston Point. There were good congregations, and the collections amounted to a con- siderably larger sum than in previous years. HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS, RHNCORNI—These schools, of which Mr. T. H. Annett is head master, still maintain the high degree of efficiency for which they have become noted. At the recent examination before Her Majesty's Inspector, Mr. S. Kianersley, 95 per cent, of the whole number of scholars have passed. The children in the sixth and seventh standards passed 100 per cent.—that is in every subject in which they were examined; whilst those in the third standard passed 100 per cent, in two subjects. THE LATE MR. WM. DOBSON* OF HIINCORN.—At the Bethesda Congregational Chapel, on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. D. Thomas preached a sermon having reference to the death of Mr. Win, Dobson. The edifice was well fibled. The rev, gentleman took for his text • "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my Lord than dwell in the tents of wickedness," and made mention of the deceased's good qualities. Appropriate hymns were sung by the choir, and on the congregation leaving the edifice Mr. Horace W. I Handley, the organist, played the "Dead March." EXCITING CHASE AT WimeEs —Yesterday afternoon P.C. Lamb was on duty near the Waterloo railway crossing, when a soldier passed him. After walking a few yards, the wearer of H.M. uniform broke into a run, and the con- , stable's suspicions being aroused, he gave chase. The officer proved to be the more speedy runner, and he came' no with his prey at the Bridge Hotel, but both pursuer and pursued were so exhausted with their exertions that neither could speak for about a minute. It then transpired that the soldier. named George Lee, was a deserter from the "King's red coats." lemecouet Snoorrien CLIIB.—The fifth monthly Shooting Clule competition took place on Saturday, at Runcorn Heath. 11 HALTON FEMALE FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—The sixty-ninth anniversary of this society was celebrated in the customary manner on Monday afternoon. Headed by the Widnes Soap Works Brass Band, 230 members walked in procession from the Castle Hotel, Halton, through the village, to the Parish Church, where a sermon appropriate to the occasion was preached by the Rev, T. M. Urmson, of Runcorn. An adjournment was then made to the Castle green, where in a tent erected by Mr. William Cooper, of Runcorn, tea pro- vided by Mr. and Mrs. Phillips, of the hotel, was partaken of. Mrs. Barrow, who has reached her 89th year, was present during the afternoon. Subsequently Mr. T. Wright apologised for the absence of Lady Brooke, the patroness, and several prominent members. The Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, stated that during the past year £BO 17s 01 had been paid in sick money. The amount received from all sources during the year had been £169 is 61. During the twelve years Mr. Wright had been secretary there had been 61 deaths, and in the same period £2,089 had been paid for sick and funeral allowances. In those 12 years 137 mem- bers had joined the society. Reference was made to the death of Mr. John Gamon, The Rey. 'l'. M. Lirmson de- livered a short address. The evening was spent in dancing to the music of the Soap Works Band.

. .- -- -- ......... ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT WIDN 0 I RS.— n Sunday morning 44 members of the Widnes Orange Lodge and some visitors walked in procession from the lodge-room. Victoria road, to Widnes Parish Church, where they attended divine service. They were adorned with the badge of the Order' and orange lilies. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams preached a sermon from the 20th verse of the fifth chapter of Matthew, He welcomed the Orangemen to Church, and thanked God for every order which sanctified its existence by the public worship of God, even though it be but once a year. Orange- men were in some instances, and he hoped in time to come they all would be amongst the formost men in the ranks of those who fought for Jesus Christ. The colour, harmless in itself, became distasteful to onlookers when they saw it worn by those who lived an ungodly life, so that the eleva- tion of the Order was in the hands of every member. They wore a colour distinctive of certain principles, notably of loyalty to God and the King, and of Holy Scripture as the infallible word of God, bat the danger was that these prin- ciples might gradually disappear, and the colour and emblem alone be left—that their religioh might begin and end in the sash they wore. Many men in the Order might say they were not guilty of formality, and so far as going regularly to church was concerned unfortunately that might be. true, to the great grief of many loyal and religious fellow mem- bers. Amongst the emblems distinctive of religious faith was the Cross of Christ, and let no one tell him that the Order condemned that glorious emblem, and considered it to be out of place upon or in a church, when it was so skilfully embroidered upon the sashes which the members wore. FUNERAL or MR. T. BALMER, OF WIDNES.—The re- mains of the late Mr. Thomas Balmer, formerly manager to Messrs Gossan'e and Sons, Widnes, were interred at the Widnes Perish Church on Saturday. The funeral cortege, consisting of a hearse and three mourning coaches, started ' from Halewood, where the deceased gentleman had resided for the past three years. In Ditton-road the members of the choirs of St. Mary's and St. Paul's Churches, under the superintendence of Mr. Crawford and Mr. Imison, took up Positions in the procession. The soap-works band, directed by Mr. Jennett, now headed the cortege, playing the De4d March, and Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., T. S. Timmis, IP., W. W. Gossage, and W. Hartland, took places in the rear when the procession reached the London and North-Western Railway Station. The churches were represented by Messrs Neil, Pankhurst, Treacy, Lord, Sm. At the church gates the body was met by the Revs. J. Wright Williams (vicar of Widnes), T. Chambersi(rector of,Halewood), A. P. Hamil- ton Wilson, and C. Rumfitt. The coffin, of polished oak, bore the following inscription :.—"Thomas Balmer, died 9th July, 1885, aged 38 years," was placed before the altar, and upon it were wreaths presented by Miss Clayden on behalf of St. Mary's School, by Miss Dunn for St. Paul's School, and by Miss Wells for her school children. The service in the interior was conducted by the ilevs. T. Chambers an 4 A. P. H. Wilson, and at the grave side the Vicar performed the burial service in the presence of a large assemblage of people. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. J. H. Lee, of Widnes. When the procession passed through the town the streets were lined with hundreds of spectators, and along the entire route there were many marks of res- pect shown. On Sunday evening the Rev, J. Wright Williams preached to a large congregation at the Parish Church, the sermon having special reference to the late Mr, Balmer.

I gROcKIRV ACCIDENT To A, eitzslllßE FArSIEN.— Mr. Thomas Charlesworth, a, well-known Cheshire agriculturist, was killed on Wedneeday in the hay-, field at Church Minshull, whilst carting hay. He observed that the bridle had slipped off a chain horse. Whilst trying to adjust it the horse started, and Mr, C'harlesworth's leg becoming entangled round the chain, he was dragged a considerable distance. He was picked Up insensible, and died a few hours afterwards. JoszEß MAzzrar, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy;" (2) "The duties of man." No pecuniary profit is desired from this publication; but it is hoped, that this eloquent memorial of anoblepatriot and a good man may awaken a true patriotic enthusiast' in the hearts of many young English readers; and that the principles set forth may help to the forma- tion of wise and just political opinions. Tho Local Government-80-a-4-1;d forwarded a general erder of regulations respecting the importation of rags from Spain, where cholera was prevalent.--,The Clerk said a similar order was issued last year and notices were sent to the Canal Company and the proprietors of the two docks to warn the Board of the arrivel of any such cargo. He would do so again. The Clerk read the! following letter whiel, was addressed to the Chairman of the Board:— "Dear sir.—Public Beths.—We beg respectfully to ask your Beard to allow us the use of the town'a water for the purposes of these baths free of Cost After the water has been used in the bens we shall be gladlo teern it into your Board's sewer for flushing purposes should you desire it. We do not want the water for oar works. We can easily supply the baths with our works' water, hut it contains a trace of iron, whieh, when the water is warmed, is precipitated and gives the water a slightly yellow tinge; to render the appearance of the water more attractive we have during the whole of last seise!) and part of the seatton before ! used the town's water at a cost of 6,1 per 1,000.. Last season ! the cot of this water was £47 lds 101. You are aware, no ! doubt. that the public have the use of these baths at a very ! small cost, and we may inform you that without counting anything for rent of land, interest on capital, depreciation of 'buildings, or for mangement, our expenditure daring the ! last five years has exceeded our receipts by nearly £lOO. This loss is almost wholly due to the charge for water, and we feir that if your Board does not grant our regteest that • we shall be obliged to revert to the use of our works water We beg to repeat that we do not ask for and do not want the water for works purposes, and only aek this con- cession in what we believe to be the public interest. Wait- ing the favour of an early reply, we are, yours truly, Gas- wino. DEACON and Co "—The Chairman said this comma- nication had been laid before the Gas Committee who had referred it to the Board. He felt that it would be-a good thing to supply the baths with water. Messrs. Ceaskell Deacon did not make any profits out of the baths, and they would not make any out of the water.—Mr. Wright said if a public body were to give water to a private coneern a very wide question would be opened up. Every ratepayer might come to the Board and tell them that something they bad in connection with the interests of the town was not paying, and ask the Board to help them out of their dlla- culties, or they would, have to increase the charges or close up. He moved that the clerk be instructed to reply that the Board could not comply with Messrs. Gaskell, Beason, and Co's request. —Mr. S. Sadler seconded the motion.— Mr. Career said if the Board did not require the water for flushing purposes the firm would use it in their works and pay the price it cost them to procure water for manufacturing purposes—al per 1,000 gallons—Mr. Handley proposed that water be sup- plied to the baths at the rate of 2d per 1,000 gallons. The baths were a public benefit, and it would be a very small matter to give the water required, but it opened up a very wide question. It was understood when the baths were built that Messrs. Gaskell would give them to the town, but some misunderstanding arose with the Board, and the transfer did not take place. The way out of the difficulty was to supply water at the price named.—Mr. B. Dutton sec mded the amendment. If the Board had the baths they would have to supply the water, and supplying the water at cheap rate would be carying out to some extent the origi- nal intentions of the Board.—Mr. Carey said the baths were filled twice a week, and on each occasion 35,000 gallons of water were used. Supposing there was any profit upon the baths, the price of admission would be at once reduced, as the firm did net wish to make a profit on the concern rebate I ever.—After some further discussion a vote was taken. For the amendment four voted, Messrs. Handley, Dutton. Brown, ' and Carey.—Mr. Handley : I don't think you should vote, Mr. Carev.—Mr. Carey : Well, it is of no interest to. me personally.—For the resolution four also voted, Messrs. Heyee, Taylor, Sadler, and Wright Mr. Carey withdrew I his vote, and the resolution not to grant the request woo de- I dared carried.

The minutes of the Highway Committee contained a letter from Messrs. T. The committee did not think it necessary to give such an assurance as if the bridge was ever built the site of the school would be required for an approach. Mr. S. B. With regard to West Bank- I street, there were several points to be considered, and the agreement would not be made until the Board had had an oppostunity of expressing an opinion upon the draft. The committee's work was not at present in a very satisfactory condition. This would' save the Board about £lOO in architect's fees, but it took the surveyor's time, and as he could not prepare plans in his office and look after the roads'and sewers both at once, the committee had decided to engage David Timperley to assist him, at a salary of 35s per week.—Mr. Sadler seconded the motion. —The Clerk here read a letter from Mr. John Matthews, leather merchant, Victoria-road, with reference to the &hock- ing sanitary condition of the cellars cP Mr. J. It was estimated that the administrative building would vast £l,OOO, bat he anticipated that it would cost nearly £1,200; but every endeavour would be made ta carry out the work for the for seer coat. 'The buildings would be ir.' accordance with the plans ant construction of epidemic) hospitals recommended is a paper contributed by Mr. Pertival Gordon Smith, the principal architect con- nected with the Local Government Board. Considering the dread- fat ravages cholera was making is Spain, and the danger of' the disease ::.`eing imported upon Brilsh shores, he was of opinion the construction of the hospital should be proceeded with at as early a date as possible.--On the motion of Mr. Heyes, seconded by Mr. Handley, a deputation consisting of' Dr. O'Keeffe„. WARRINGTON BOROUGH. COURT. Siermiliay.—Before Alderman Burgess. DRl7Nloll4NEB9.—ltichard Molitor was sent to gaol for seven days for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick- street the previous evening. MONDAY.—Erefore Alderman Harrison and Councillor Greening. A LAZY VAGRANT.—Aaron Grubbier was sent to prison for 14 days for refusing to break stones while a casual in- mate of the vagrant wards at the Workhouse. A DESERTER.—James Hatton, a deserter from the Bth Hussars, stationed at Dublin, on the sth July, was re- manded to Walton. MISCELLANEGUS.—The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—John MacMahon, in Church-street, on Saturday night, sent to prison for a month ; Dominick Knoelston, in Bridge-street, on Sunday, fined 5s and costs ; John Galvin, in Friars' Green, on Saturday, sent to prison for a month; Margaret aeetor, in Orford-lane, on the 28th tilt, fined lOs and costs; Edward Carney, in Sankey-atreet, on Sunday, fined 5s including costs; Samuel Williams, in Buttermarket-street, on the 4th lust, fined 5s and costs : Robert Thornlev, in Gilbert-street, on the sth mat, fined 5s including cost ; John Flaherty, for drunkenness and for assaulting P.C. Johnson, was fined 10s and costa.—A charge of stone throwing against Bridget Toole and Catherine Garrity was withdrawn in consequence of the non-appearance of a witm-ss. OVERCROWDING.—Thomas Chatters and James Worrell were summoned by Assistant Inspector. French for keeping lodgers without having their dwelling-houses registered— Both seemed to have inadvertently broken the law, and they were only ordered to pay costa. Farmix.—Before Captain Reynolds (in the chair), Dr. _ .

Gornall, and Mr. H. Garnett. MISCELIANEOUS.—Mary Goodier, the Seven Stars, Bridge- street, was fined is and costs for allowing a deposit of garb- age on her premises. The offence was committed during the temporary absence from home of Mrs Gaudier—James Burns was summoned .by John Gallop for absenting him- self from his employ as an apprentice of the latter. The case was adjourned for a fortnight to allow the defendant an opportunity of returning to work. ASSILTILTING A CONSTABLE.—John Stirrup, jun., labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in St. James's- street on the 11th inst., and assaulting P.C. Bell. The officer was in plain clothes, going home, and when on Latch- ford-road he heard what seemed to boa policeman's whistle, and went to a group of men who were making a dis- turbance. He advised them to be quiet, and defendant, remarking that the constable wanted a "COP," assaulted him by striking him on the head and face. Defendant denied that it was he who committed the asQault, and said he was merely watching the row. He was fined 103 and costs for assaulting the police, and ordered to pay the cost of the summons for being drunk.

DISORDERLY PERSONS.—Jane Oliver, of Fryer-street, was fined lOs and costs, 12e 61, for making use of profane lan- guage in Fryer-street, on the 29th June.—Patrick Brereton, Evan Evans, and Margaret Royle were each fined for being drunk and disorderly. WATER RA.TES.—Thirty-two persons were summoned by the Water Company for non.payment of rates due for water Thirty cases were settled out of court, and an order for payment in 14 days was made in the remaining two. Fnatous RlDlSG.—Robert Spencer, a boatman, was charged with furiously riding a horse.—P.C. Smith stated that on the sth inst ha saw the defendant riding a horse very furiously up Bridge-street. He was beating the animal with a rope.—A fine of 5s and costs, lie 6d, was im- posed.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. Nostay—Before Mr. U.S. Hall and Mr. T. S. Timrnis. DRUNKENNESS.— For this offence Patrick Grady, Mar- garet Cunningham, Michael Wilson, and Bernard Cullen were each fined. THEFT OF BurrEß.—Mary Cooney, a married woman, was charged with having on the 7th inst. stolen gibs. of butter, value 6e, the property of John Connolly, grocer, Brynne-street. The circumstances have been reported, and the prisoner, who has previously been convicted, pleading gnilty, she was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.

Hall. DISORDERLY CHARACTERS—For being drunk the fol- lowing 'Arsons were each fined r—Bridgst Campbell, Mary Riley, Margaret Redmond, Edward Lawton, John Curley. Joseph Benyon, carter, St. Helens, was, on the evidence of Superintendent Barker, fined 103 and costs 7s 6d for being drunk in charge of two horses and a cart on the sth inst. Ellen Atherton was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for sleeping in an outhouse in Mersey-road on the previous night. For begging in Lngsdale-road on the previous day Bridget Thompson, a tramp, was sent to gaol for seven days. Jane Kilroy and Ellen Cross were charged with committing a breach of the peace at Dillon on the 6th inst. The case against Kilroy was dismissed, and Cross was bound over in the usual sureties. Twinsry GREENGROCEUS.—CharIes Clifton, greengrocer, Waterloo-road, Widnes, and James Devenport, greengrocer's assistant, Warrington. were charged with obstructing Lugsdale-road by leaving their carts there an unreasonable time on the afternoon of the 3rd inst. P.S. Strickland proved that the defendants were ten minutes in the Market Hotel whilst their carts were standing in the roadway. Each defendant was fined 5s and costs 49 6d.

THE WIMBLEDON MaETP.M—At Wimbledon on Tuesday competition for the Qaeen's Prize commenced, and acme very good shooting was made. Private Fidler, let Berks ; Private Ridgway, London Rifle Brigade; Lieutenant Glen, Inns of Court ; and Private Aston, 2nd Worcestershire, all made within one point of the highest possible in seven shots at 200 yards. Some members of the Canadian team were conspicuous among the leading three hundred. For the Alfred Prize five competitors tied with scores of 32 points each. Shooting for the Queen's Prize at Wimbledon was resumed on Wednesday morning under conditions so favour- able that two highest possible scores were made by Lieuten- ant Lock and Private N,.:wns, both of the let Surrey,at 500 yards before ten o'clo,k. After that the wind became very variable, and many competitors who had stood high on the list on the first day fell so far back as to completely spoil their chance. In the revolver competition Major Scott Glendinning put five shots within the three inch bull's- eye, and only just missed that mark by its own breadth with his sixth shot. On Thursday the shooting for the Queen's Prize (preliminary sfwe) was concluded. The competitors have fired at the 200, 500, and 600 yards ranges, and the first three hundred men on the list of scorcs will now com- pete for places in the Sixty" who enzage in the final struggle for her Majesty's gift and oi her substantial re- wards. There was a large entry of volunteer marksmen from Lancashire and Cheshire, but few of them have secured a place in the 300. It unluckily happened that a heavy rainstorm, with a gusty wind, passed over the common whilst the men from, these two counties were firing, and many promising scores made a,t shorter ranges were thus Thin--six local volunteers shot so well, however, that they will be included in the "300," with an oppor- tunity or gaining adm!ssion to the Sixty. It is stated that the title by which Sir Baliol Brett, Master of the Rolla, will be raised to the peerage is that of Lord Esher. ST. HELENS SWIATING CLI7I3.—A. week or two ago a club to be known as the St. Helens Amateur Swimming Club was formed, and up to the present about 40 persons have been elected members. His worship the Mayor (Alderman r. Cook) bas been appointed president, and Councillors Gamble. Brown Ellison, Forster, Wilcock, Foster, E. Johnson, and Brook vice-presidents. Mr. T. D. McKenzie has been elected hon. secretary, and Mr. John S. Mather hon, treasurer, while the following have been elected as a committee i—Messrs. IL Lomax, Bandon, Thomas, W. Ray, Woods, and J. Hall. The " opening night" for the season was Tuesday evening, when by the kindness of the Corporation the members of the club had the exclusive use of the plunge bath. A goodly number of swimmers attended, and there was a large attendance of interested spectators. _

THE " PALL MALL GAZETTE."—PROCEEDINGS AGAINST NEWSVENDOES.—Some lads were charged in Glasgow, on Saturday, with selling what purports to be reprints of Pall Mall Gazette, containing recent disclosures. The Stipen- diary-General did not think there was any charge against the boys. They were selling a copy of an article in a newspaper which exposed what was said to be true. The boys were discharged.—On Monday, before Mr. Raffles, at the Liverpool Pol ce Court, Michael Berry, of Manchester, was charged under the Liverpool Police Act with selling an obscene publication in the streets.—Mr. Marks, prosecuting solicitor, said the prisoner was seen standing at the corner of Bold-street and Hanover-street on Saturday afternoon offering for sale a publication of an obscene character. A constable parchased a copy, and after seems the nature of it he took the prisoner to the Detective-office. The prisoner gave a false address. The publication professed to be a re- print of articles which recently appeared in the Pall Mall Gazette, and the prisoner had in his possession a large num- ber of copies. Upon examination it was seen that every- thing which was decent in the original articles in the news- paper had been omitted, and only the objectionable and obscene parts retalned.—Police-constable 356 gave evidence of arrest, and said the prisoner was calling oat at the top of his voice, "Pall Mall Gazette. Shocking revelations. Two- pence each."—Mr. Raffl s Whatever may be said for the Pall Nall Gazette and its object in publishing these articles, there can be no excuse for selling these extracts. The ob- ject of publishing these extracts can only be to pander to the tastes of filthy-minded people. Ido not decide the question between that journal and the public; that has to be settred hereafter. In the meantime I shall fine the pri- soner 20e arid costs, or in default fourteen days' hard labour. —William Hannon, a youth, was also fined 20s and coats for selling the pamphlets in Lime-street on Saturday night at half-past eleven o'clock. Detective McConchie said the prigoner was selling the copies at sixpence each.—On Wed- nesday, the 23 newsboys charged by the City Solicitor with causing an obstruction through selling an immoral publication appeared on remand at the Mansion House be- fore the Lord Mayor, who decided that as the Government did not intend to prosecute the publishers he could not pro- ceed with the charge against these defendants.

EDMUND KNOWLES MUSPRATT, F.C.S.

The following sketch of the career of Mr. E. K. Muspratt, which we take from the Biograph, will be read with especial, interest in view of his having been selected as the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division.

The subject of the present sketch, is the youngest son of James Muspratt, of Liverpool, and was born at Linacre, near Liverpool, in 1833. He was educa- ted at the Pestalozzian Institution, Worksop, under the direction of Dr. Heldenmaier, a pupil of Pesta- lozzi. The Pestalotziaii system of education bears about the same relation to the antique methods, h .whicwere popular at that time, as does the Baco- nian method to the elder methods of philo§ophical enquiry. The leading feature of the Pestalozzian schools was"the inculcation of instruction by means of "object lessons," thus bringing earlyinto play the observant and the reasoning faculties. In 1850, Mr. Muspratt went to Giessen to study chemis- try under Baron Liebig, and in the year 1&53 en- tered the University of Munich, as the eminent chemist removed to that city, having accepted the Professorship of Chemistry there. At the sugges- tion of Baron Liebig he followed the regular medi- cal course, with a view of devoting himself to the study of• Physiological Chemistry. What results might have accrued to science and humanity, how much physical suffering might have been evaded or alleviated, bad this resolve met IV t h no

disturbing influence we cannot determine' ; but viewing what has been achieved by Mr. Muspratt in the sphere he has filled, we cannot but think much distinction would have been earned by him in the other walk of life. Mr. Muspratt's immedi- ate ancestor was also the "father of the alkali manufacture of England," and in 1856, he was called from Germany to undertake the management of his father's alkali works in Liverpool. Under his fostering care, and that of the Muspratt family, the alkali manufacture has, grown and flourished. To- day, Widnes, St. Helens, the Tyneside, Glasgow, and Flint, are the large and important centres of its activity. It has become a source of national wealth, eclipsed only by the older iron and cotton indus- tries. Still the Muspratt family are at the head of the trade, their joint works being larger than those of any other manufacturers, that at Flint alone having only one rival in size, viz., the extensive works of Messrs. Tennant at Glasgow. This is vert largely due to the exertions of Mr. E. K. Muspratt, who, at the joint offices of the three works in Liverpool, has personally conducted their large business operations extending over this kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zea- land. Besides this, he has kept vigilant watch and direction over the manufacturing processes at Liverpool and Widnes, which requires not only theoretical knowledge of the processes in use, but also practical acquaintance with the necessary varied manipulation. Some idea of the value of the alkali trade to civilisation may be gained by a brief survey of its position prior to the time of the senior Mr. Muspratt, and the influence which its extension has had upon old industries or in :the creation of new ones. The original source of car- bonate of soda, the staple product of the alkali manufacture, was the seaweed which exists round our sea coast. This seaweed; collected principally on the coasts of Scotland and the Orkney and Shet- land islands, was first burnt, and the soluble matter, chiefly carbonated of soda, extracted from the ash by solution. The liquors thus obtained were boiled down, and the solid matter thus ob- tained further shied by heating it in furnaces; this crude carbonate of soda then passed into commerce, under the names of kelp, barilta, or varee. The grow- ing demand for glass, which followed upon the abolition of the window tax, had doubtless much influence in determining the efforts which resulted in the present process of radnufacture. The process followed to-day is that of Leblanc, and is essentially this: sulphate of soda, limestone (carbonate of lime), and slack (carbon) are roasted to-. gether, the melted mass so obtained, consists prin- cipally of carbonate of soda and sulphide of limp, and is known as black ash or British barilla. It is subjected to treatment similar in every respect to that previously applied to seaweed ashes.. From. the carbonate of soda liquors at first obtained, another modification of soda, viz., caustic soda, is also manufactured in great quantity. Upon the rapid, regular, and economical production of carbon- ate of soda and caustic soda, depends the well-being of our extensive glass and soap manufactures, and , the production of our daily newspaper. That Mr. Muspratt might have made a more dazzling personal'reputation had he followed' out) his original course of study may be granted; it is, however, doubtful if it would have equalled the regard which cannot be withheld from one who has done so much to foster those practical arts on which so much of national prosperity and civiliza- tion depend. ' Mr. Muspratt's outward man bears the strong and unmistakeable impress of the qualities which he possesses. An active, lithe figure, carried forward by firm, rapid, and yet nervous strides, surmounted by a dark and somewhat long and thoughtful vis- age, with restless piercing eyes, and clear cut nose, beneath which is a firm mouth, with just a sugges- tion of curve at'its corners; these indicate a man naturally fitted to organise and control exten- sive undertakings, and not to be easily misled or chicaned. "Besides the advantage of the scientific training Which Germany afforded him, Mr. Muspratt enjoyed the inestimable privilege of intimate association with the band of remarkable men in every path of literature and science, drawn to the Bavarian Capi- tal by thelate king Maximilian. Subsequently to his return to England, he dis- played a strong interest in political questions, and particularly in political economy, and was much in- fluenced by the works of John Stuart Mill. The active assistance which Mr. Muspratt has rendered to various commercial, economical, and social move- ments may be gleaned from the subsequent para- graphs. In 1858, he joined the Council of the Financial Reform Association, and in 1860 was elected treasurer, on the retirement of the late Mr. John Smith. For the past 20 years he has taken an active part in the work of the association, and is now its president. In 1860 he represented the Lancashire branch of the Alkali Manufacturers' Association, during the negotiation of the Anglo- French Treaty of Commerce, and at the request of Mr. Cobden gave evidence before the Conseil Superieur du Commerce on the relative cost of chemical pyoducts in France and England. In the same year-Mr. Muspratt was elected to thq Council of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, and in 1865 represented that body at Vienna, during the negotiations for a commercial treaty. On his re- turn he presented a report on the commercial and industrial position of Austria to the Chamber. The reform of the national weights and measures, and the decimalization of our coinage, have obtained a large share of his attention. In common with other Englishmen who took part in the Anglo-French Treaty negotiations, he was much struek with the simplicity and accuracy of the French calculations of the cost of manufacture due to their admirable metric system. On his return to England he took every opportunity of giving support to the move- ment carried on by Mr. James Yates and Professor Leone Levi, in favour of the adoption of the metric system by this country. At the Conferences on In- ternational Coinage in Paris in 1867, he represented the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, and drew up a report on the subject, which was presented to the Chamber, and in 1868 gave evidence on behalf of the Chamber before the Royal Commission on Interna- tional Coinage, advocating a system of international gold coinage on the basis of the dollar unit, equal to five francs, the English sovereign to be made equal to five dollars, cir twenty-five franci. Mr. Muspratt has arso given evidence before the Select Committee on Letter's Patent for Inventions, and the Royal Commissions on the Pollution of Rivers and Noxious Vapours. In- these his special knowledge renderedhis evidence, ungrudgingly and minutely given, of more than ordinary value. In connection with the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce he has been for many years Chairman of the Horne Trade, and Railway Committee, and the year 1875 was elected President. He also took a prominent part in memorializing the Government for a reform and simplification of the tariff by the abolition of the corn, sugar, and tea duties, &c., and the consolidation of the Customs and Excise depart- ments. Many of these reforms have been ef- ected, and it is to be hoped that the others will follow. It would be a Matter for astonishment, if the business-like and practical insight and capacity ,fon productive work thus displayed, had been allowed to pass without some recognition„ In 1877, and at 4 critical juncture in local municipal affairs, Mr. Muspratt was requested by an influential "deputation of ratepayers to contest St. Peter's ward, on the retirement of Mr. Beloe, and was returned unop- posed; and in last November, when every ward was contested, he was again returned by a large majority. Always a Liberal of the advanced and—not to put too tine a pqint on it—,democratic (lifter, Mus- pratt has, by reason of 'his native intelliggnce, al-

The contest between North and South at Old Trafford was throughout splendidly contested and exciting. The scores were :—Nortb, 192 and 366; South, 183 and 114. At Lord's Ground on Saturday, amidst a scene ot excite- ment, and. alter a splendidly contested game, Elarrew proved victorious in their encounter with Eton, the winning hit being only made within three minutes of time. Notts v. Yorkshire have this week met at Trent Bridge, the opposing teams being the same as those which played at Sheffield in their first encounter. Hall beat Shaw for ' choice of innings, and sent in his team to bat, who held possession of the ground all Monday afternoon and until twenty minutes after luncheon interval on Tuesday, when the innings closed for 424. At the close of the second day's play eight of the Notts wickets had fallen for 166 rune. In the face of such a deficit nothing but a follow- on could be expected, and therefore took place. The second innings of Notts realised 209, and the result of the match was the defeat of Notts by an innings and 28

At Brighton the return match between Surrey and Sussex was played, the visitors going in to bat first. The innings eventually closed for 501. The Sussex innings reached 209, and a follow-on ensued. The match ended in a one Inning's defeat and 124 runs to spare for Sussex. In the Middlesex and Kent match, the metropolitan county put together 336 during Monday afternoon, Mr. G. B. &add putting on 104 in admirable style. Kent compiled 191, and of course had to follow On. Their second essay fell short of the first by three runs, and Middlesex won by ten wickets.

The match between Cheshire and Leicestershire, that ended at Leicester on Tuesday, was in favour of the home county by an innings and 25 runs. With eight wickets down for 209 runs, Leicestershire continued their innings with Bettomore and Rylott, the not outs. The former put together 38 before his wicket was claimed, and the innings closed for 261. With 169 runs to the bad Cheshire began their second innings, but the bowling of Rylott and Pougher was very effective, the former claiming five wickets for 44 runs and the latter four for 34. The innings closed for 134, with the above-mentioned result.

div.head: LOCAL EMBEZZLEMENT CASE.
div.p: LOCAL EMBEZZLEMENT CASE.

At theJaiverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mn Baffles, stipendiary magistrate, Frederick Augustus Herr-- son, a middle-aged man, who some time ago was a relieving officer in the Prescot Union, appeared on bail to answer a charge of having embezzled several sums of money belong- ing to his employer, Henry Leon Stern, a cigar dealer, carrying on business at 37, South Castle-street, Liverpool. Mr. Marks prosecuted, and Mr. Mearns (St. Helens)tap- peered on the prisoner's behalf. In opening the case Mr. Marks stated that about twelve months ago prosecutor engaged the prisoner as traveller and collector, the under. standing being that he was to travel for Mr. Stern alone, and that he was to receive a wage varying with the profits, which was a commission on the amounts collected. At the end of the half year (June) Mr Stern sent out a number of , notes to his various customers who, he believed, owed him money at that time. He thereup.n received a large number of replies denying any indebtedness whatever on the pert of the customers, who stated their willingness to produce receipts which had been given by the prisoner. Mr. Stern thereupon made some inquiries, and found there was a total deficiency in his business of LIST, and he at once took steps to have the prisoner brought before the magistrates.— Mr. Stern, the prosecutor, then gave evidence, and explained that prisoner's duties were to solicit;orders, collect money due, and account to witness every Saturday. When first spoken to by witness about failing to account for money, the accused said the deficiencies only amounted to about £3O, but it was afterwards found that the deficiencies amounted to over .£l57.—A number of publican's from War- rington, Chester, and Widnes were next examined as to their having pad to the prisoner sums of money which he had never accunted for. One of these witnesses, a person named Peter Davies Taylor, of the Clapgate Hotel, Widnes, produced the following letter, which he had received from Harrison, and which was read in court :—" 37. South Castle-street, Liverpool, Saturday evening.—Dear Taylor,— told my boss I had left Whittield's cigars".;with you, and be thought he could not do better than transfer them to you, but I will see on Monday or Tuesday morning about them, and allow you a good reduction. Don't do anything with them till I see you.—Yours lovingly, F. A. HARRISON, nap-player." (Laughter.)—Mr. Marks: What did he mean by nap-player? Witness: It was only a joke.—Mr. Marks : That may be, but it may serve to give some indi- cation as to where the money has gone.—Detective Hob. bins stated that, in company with Detective Moore, he ar- rested the prisoner on the 6th inst., and when charged with embezzlement the accused said, "I am not guilty ; I used the money in the business."—The prisoner, who reserved his defence, was then committed to the Sessions for trial, two bails of £5O each being accepted for his appearance.

The Duke of Connaught has been suffering from bay fever, and in his case the symptoms are so severe as to affect his voice.

A terrible fire bas taken place in the Russian town of Kursk. More than a hundred houses were burned to the ground within a quarter of an hour. The Kirklands Hotel, Kinross, a great resort of Loch Leven anglers, was on Wednesday ni4ht destroyed by fire. Mrs. Small, a spectator, fell down from excitement, and instantly expired. A select committee of the House of Lords, on Thursday ailernooon, passed the Manchester and Middleton District Tramways Bill, which authorises the expenditure of £60,000 on tramways. Pm MEN DROWNED.—Off Gravesend. on Thursday morning, the steamer Penedo, belonging to Messrs. Payman, Bell, and Co., of Newcastle, collided with and sank the schooner Bertha, Of Guernsey, whose crew of five men were drowned.

The Central News is authorised to state that Mr. Cita:, stone is not suffering from sore throat, but is simply taking advantage of a period of rest to have his throat attended to in view of the hoarseness with which be has been troubted of late. Dr. Clarke is in attendance. . FATAL ACCIDENT IN THE ALPS.—A report from Genev,i says that the Vice-President of the French Alpine Club, M. Chifflet, lids been found dead with his two guides at the foot of the Glacier do Col d'Argentiere, Mont Blanc, Six hours distance from Chamounix. The guides were one of, the most experienced men in Chamonnix and his son. ~ FRIGHTFUL DEATH.-0E Saturday. while Jslna Cart- wright was directing some miners in their work at the Old Park Colliery, Lower Gornal, a sudden bump occurred, and a large piece of coal fell from the roof, crushing the de- ceased into the ground. He was frightfully injured, his ribs protruding into the lungs, and he died when being re- moved to his home.

WESLKYANS IN PARLILMENT.—Mr. Henry Atkinson, the new Conservative member for North Lincolnshire, is a lead• log member of the Wesleyan body. The other members of Parliament who are Wesleyans are the following :—Sir W. M'Arthur, Mr. A. M'Arthur, Mr. S. D. Waddy, Mr. E. Bald- win, Mr. A. Brogdeu, Mr. J. C. Clarke, Mr. H. H. Fowler, and Mr. W. S. Allen—all Liberals.

ways held aloof from mere servile, party allegiance, I or the dictates of personal ambition. It must be I remembered to his credit, that when the death of Mr. Ellis Eyton caused a vacancy for the borough of Flint, where his influence and that of his family, as employers and landowners, are almost paranfount, and where his many services to the Liberal cause could not fail to be known and appreciated—Mr. Muspratt, without hesitation or ostentation, with- drew a candidature which at least must have been powerful, when it was signified that John Roberts, Esq., of Liverpool, would receive the support of the party.

_ As a speaker, Mr. Muspratt may perhaps not claim to rank among oar orators, but he is invalua- ble in debate, enunciating clearly, forcibly, 4nd un- erringly his own vieWs, and keeping the matter under discussion Tree from irrelevant or disturbing side-influences. With his proved business ability, his keen and practical sympathy with and experi- ence of practical reform and public business it will be to us a matter of more than ordinary surprise, if he be not called upon at some time not far distant to fill a seat in Parliament

We may add to the abo've interesting sketch from the Biograph that Mr. Muspratt was married in 1861 to Frances, eldest daughter of Thomas Baines, Esq., and niece of Sir Edward Baines, of Leeds; and that during the present year the Society of Chemical Industry did him thd distinguished honour of elect- ing him to be President of the Society.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

SCHOOX, Taxims.—.-On Monday afternoon the town was en fete, the occasion being the annual field days given to the various Sunday schools. The children mustered in great numbers, and marched from their several school rooms to Knowsley Park (kindly thrown open to them for the day - by Lord Derby), with flags od banners, and bands playing. During the afternoon iames of various kinds were indulged in, and prizes given. The Weslevans numbered between 500 and 600 children, end the adults were led by the Rev. John Shipharn and Mr. Leadbetter, superintendent. On the way they stopped at the residence of the Rev. B. Varley and sang a hymn; afterwards they entered the park by the Eccleston Lodge, as Sid also the Victoria Place Sunday School, numbering about 200, who were accompanied by the Rev. C. Wesley Hopper, Mr. Willis. and Mr. WycherleY• The Zion School was preceded by the Whiston brass band ; and the Holy Cross Catholic School by their drum and fife band entered the park by the Present Lodge. DE4TH O THB, REV. B. VARLBY.—On Thursday after- noon, at half•paat fivo,o'clock, the death took place at his late residence, Ward-street, Prescot, of a well known rev. gentleman who will be missed from the town and ne;gh- bourhood, and from the Wesleyan circles in particular. He died after a fortnight's illness frpm congestion of the lungs, at the age of 43. He had been connected with the Pre,pot Wesleyan chapel for nearly twelve months, having come horn Huyton Quarry on their invitation. He was a very effective preacher and an indomitable worker, though for the last seven years he had been totally blind. Be wa, educated at Didsbury College, where he peeled the crime- nations in the first class. He was many years connected with the Grove-street Circuit, Liverpool. His sympathies were always shown in any good cause irrespective of sect or party. One of the latest of his public appearances was at the bazaar lately held by the United Free Methodists, when ,he took part in the opening ceremony. Be /eaves a widow, but no family.
_ THE ROYAL Saow.—Misa Ward, daughter of Mr. Otti- well Ward, Halahead Hall Farm, has taken the first prize for dairymaid at the Royal Show at Preston.

div.head: GENERa NEWS.
div.p: GENERa NEWS.

Mr. Trevelyan. addrresed a meeting at Leamington, on Wednesday night, and dealt almost exclusively with the probable issue of the approaching general election. The Guards' Camel Corps, returning from Egypt, landed at Cowes on Wednesday morning, and were subsequen'l9 paraded before Osborne House, where they were inspected by the Queen. _ _
The Munster Bank has been compelled to stop payment, owing to the " ran " upon its funds which set in after a recent legal decision. It is stated that the assets will fully meet the liabilities.

In the case of Gerhardt v. the Great Northern Railway Company, heard on Wednesday, in London, the plaintiff MO awarded £4,000 damages far injuries which he sustained in a collision on the defendant company's line in 1881. At the Royton Police Court, on Wednesday, Richard Edmund Fitton, late salesman for the Shaw Spinning Com- pany Limited, Oldham, was committed for trial on a charge of falsifying his books and embezzlin4 'various sums of money amounting to £9OO. Srarroorare WITH A 13nreurAra.—A. desperate encounter took place early on Tuesday morning between a policeman and a burglar on the root of a house in Kensington Park Gardens, London. The constable, a young fellow named Owen, discovered the burglar, and attempted to arrest him. The burglar replied with several pistol shots, one of which took effect in Owen's throat. His assailant escaped. ALLEGED CHILD MURDER.—The Manchester Stipendiary, on Wednesday, remanded a young woman, named Elizabeth Lane, On a charge of having drowned her illegitimate baby. Prisoner, who worked as a match-box maker, left her lodg- ings on Sunday evening, taking the child with her. She Was seen with the baby near the Rochdale canal at Ancoats, where the body was found on Tuesday.. On returning to her lodgings thd prisoner said she had left the infant with its father. THR PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF WALES visited Leeds On Wednesday, and opened the Yorkshire College, which has recently been built in that town at a cost of £67,000. Their Royal Highnesses were received with much cordiality by the people. An address was presented to the Prince and Princess by the Mayor and Corporation, and the chief Mil- cars of the local Masonic lodges offered a hearty welcome to the Worshipful Grand Master of the Order. On reaching the College the Prince and Princess inspected the several departments of the building. THE CLIFTON HALL COLLIERY EXIMOSION.—MEDALS FOR THE EXELOREES.—At a recent, meeting of the Humans Society for the hundred of Salford, it was resolved that six gold medals be presented to the same number of the most deserving of the exploring or rescuing party at the late ex- plosion at Clifton Hall Colliery—the selection to be made by Mr. Pickard, secretary? of the Miner's Association. It was also decided by the society to do away with their present medal, and Alderman Batley was instructed to design a new pattern, the first six of which will be distributed in the above canse at the next annual meeting of the society. SUICIDE OF A YARN AGENT AT HASLINGDEN.—EarIy on Tuesday morning, the body of H. Chappel, aged 57 years, a Manchester commission yarn agent, WAS discovered floating in the Reservoir of Acre Mill. Deceased, who was a widower with seven children, resided at Clough End, near Haslineden, and retired to rest at eleven o'clock on Monday 'night. The right hon. gentleman sent in reply the following letter :—"4O, Prince's-gardens, S.W., ' July 9th, 1835. Dear sir,—la reply to your favour of the Bth inst. I can only sav that under the Bankruptcy Act any creditor to the extent of £5O, or any number of creditors , whose joint de,bts amount to that sum, can prevent a private ' airangement and secure a public investigation. Ido not think the law can do more than this for the protection of creditors ; and if they prefer a private arran;enaent with all the experience of the past to a public inquiry, I do not know • how it is to be prevented. Th 3 experience, however, of the working of the present Act shows that In a great number of • cases where private arrangements have been proposed and rejected, bankruptcy has produced much Setter result.— Yours truly, J. CHAMBERLAIN." WIT AND HUMOUR. A VANE BIRD—The weather-cock. Carus OPERATION.—Kissing a lady's snowy brow. ALWATs ImaiERSED IN BUSINESS.— teachers of swimming. No man of honour can steal a kiss from a girl when he can just as well give her one. In India a widow burns for her first husband. In this country she burns for a second one. When is a tree like a boarder at a summer hotel minus funds? When its trunk is serzed for board. It seems no more than right that men should seize Time by the forelock, for the rude old fellow sooner or later pulls all their hair out. "Yes," said Jones, 'when my wife gets mad she reminds me of a vessel under weigh." "flow so ?" inquired Smith. "Because she's got her rancour up." Blind man who is about to be married: "I wad gie a , launder pound' tae see her "—i e, his wife that is to be.— Triend : " Nae doubt ye wad the coo, but wait till ye're marrit—she'll open your een for ye !" In a market town in the North the following placard is affixed to the shutters of a watchmaker who has decampsd, leaving his creaitors miens—" Wound up, and the main- spring broke." Scene—New York theatre. Countryman at box-office: Gimme two seats.—Treasurer: Do you want contiguous seats ?—Conntryman: No, sir. lam on my weddin'-towce, an' nuthin' but the best goes. Gimme orchestra-chairs. Cams OF HAIRLESS PATES.—" If I ever marry, I shan't seek for mind; mind is too cold. I shall choose an emo- tional woman." "Don't du it," eagerly exclaimed his bald- headed friend, suggestively pointing to his hairless pate— don't do it, I implore you! My wife is an emotional , woman !" VIRTUE'S REWAED.—A traveller in New Zealand, re- visiting:a native village after some months' absence, and miming a well-meaning but rather tedious Maori, inquired what had become of him. " Ah," said the village chief I Mournfully, "he gave us so much good advice that we had to Put him to death mercifully !" A young five-year-old hopeful was playing on the lawn With his sister, when he slipped and fell. Springing op, he began to belabour his companion with ungentlemanly fierce- ness, crying out, " If I did stand on your shadow, was that any reason why you should drag it away from under me BO ' 58 to throw me off my feet ?" A youthful Hebrew was discovered by hishorrified parents to have developed a fancy for that succulent dish upon the origin of which the gentle Ella so charmingly descants. The rabbi was consulted, the suggestion being that the youngster was mad. The holy man dissented from that view, saying that, although the action was sinful, it was no sign of aberration of the intellect. Soon again came the parents, this time more alarmed than ever, their son and heir having been discovered performing an osculatory 1 Process upon the face of the Gentile handmaid. "Assuredly," 1 they said, he must be mad !" But the p: iest was still nn- ' convinced. "Son and daughter," he said, "there is certainly much evil in the young man's disposition; but I find no evidence of insanity. If he gad kissed the pork and eaten the gill, I should have thought him mad indeed!" A half-naked Indian was looking on at some workmen in the employ of Governor Dudley of Massachusetts. "Why don't you work and get yourself some clothes?" asked the governor. "Why don't you work ?" retorted the son of the forest. "I work head-work," said Dudley, pointing to his head. The Indian said he was willing to work, and agreed to kill a calf for the governor. Having done so, he came for his pay. !. But," said the governor," you have not dressed the calf." "No," said the Indian; "I was to have a 1 for killing him. Am he no dead, governor ?" t' mding himself outwitted, the governor gave him another Slialing for dressing it. It was not long before the Indian Came back demanding a good shilling in place of the bad one which he declared the governor had paid him. The governor paid him another. Returning with still another brass piece to be changed, the governor, convinced of his knavery, offered him half-a-crown if he would deliver a letter for him. The letter was directed to the keeper of the prison, and ordered him to give the bearer a certain number of lashes. The Indian, suspecting that all was not right, and meeting a servant of the governor, induced him to take the letter to his address. The result Of the Indian's stratagem was that a severe whipping was administered to tiae unfortunate servant. The governor was greitly chagrined at being a second time outwitted by the Indian. On falling in with him some time after, he accosted him With severity, asking him how he had dared to cheat and deceive him so many times. "Head-work, governor— head-work !" was the reply. A census enumerator on calli,ng at a house was received by a stiff, well-dressed lady, who could well be recognised as a widow of some years standing. He inquired for the tUnber of persons in the family. "Eight, sir," replied the "including myself." "Very well—your age, madam?" .; my age, sir," replied the lady with a piercing, dignified tOok," I conceive it's none of your business what my age May be; you are inquisitive, sir." "The law, compels me, madam, to take the age of every person in the ward; it's my dotY to make the inquiry." "Well, if the law compels you to ask, I presume it compels me to answer. I sin between F'lirty and forty." "I presume that means thirty-five." No, sir, it means no such thing; I am only thirty-three Years of age." "Very well, madam," putting down the fi.gures, "just as you say. Now for the age of the children, commencing with the youngest, if you please." "Josephine, my youngest, is ten years of age.' "Josephine—pretty flame—ten." "Minerva was twelve last week." "Minerva --captivating—twelve." "Cleopatra Elvira has just turned Afteen, and Angelina is eighteen, just eighteen." " Ange- lina—favourite name—eighteen." "My eldest, and only married daughter, sir, Anne Si)phia, is a little over twenty- " Twenty-five, did you say, madam ?" "Yes, sir, is there anything remarkable in her beingof that age ?" ,)ao, I can't say there is; but it is remarkable that you should ne her mother when you were only eight years of age !" About that time the census-taker was observed running out Of the house, closely pursued by a broomstick. It was the last time he pressed a lady to give her exact age. ---------

TRE ALLEGED FRAUDULENT BANK- RUPTCY AT WAIIRINGTON., , At Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday, Richard Spano, wheelwright, formerly tarrying on business at Friars' Green, was brought up on remand, before Council- lor Greening and Mr. Monks, charged with having on the 4th March, within four months of the presentation of his bankruptcy petition, fraudulently removed divers of his goods, to the value of £lO and upwards, contrary to sub- section t, section 11, of the Debtors' Act, 1889, in conceal- ing part of his property to the amount of £lO and upwards; and in making a material omission in a statement relating to his affairs. Mr. P. Davies, instructed by the Treasury, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. Censiderable in-. terest in the proceedings was manifes ed by the public.— Ins.pecter Spinks, of the borough police force, stated that he apprehended prisoner, who said " It's a bad job, I have nothing further to say at present."—Sarah Chapman, wife of James Chapman, Willesten, Nantwich, said she remem- bered the night of the 17th March, when her husband was at Spann's all night. She went to Spann's about six o'clock next morning, and asked if her husband was there. Spann said that be was, and she must go away and not make a noise. Later on she met Spann in Mersey-street and asked hies what sort of a Man he called himself to get her husband to sign a paper to the effect that he bad received his wages. Spann teld her to hold her noise, or she would get him locked up.—David Rankin' manager for Messrs. Scales and Salter, said that on the sth March he saw James Chapman, Joseph Bridge, and a boy pass his shop in Bridge-street, with a truck laden with large pieces of timber.—P.G. Bild• endale repeated evidence given by him at the County Court examination.—Joseph Bridge, recalled, said that he remem- bered the day on whicn Spann was adjudicated a bankrupt. A few days previous witness went to the house of John Cross in Rose and Crown-street. There he saw John and Joseph Cross, and afterwards prisoner, who said 'Does thou know anything about what Chapman is doing." He had a paper in his hand. Witness said they were aware of what Chapman had been swearing. Prisoner said "Listen to this and see whether this is it that Chapman has been swearing, and whether it is true or not." Prisoner read extracts, and witness told him it was true what Chapman had said. Pri- soner said "Has thou took the oath that this is correct," and witness said that he had not taken say oath. Prisoner then said " Then thy word is as good as his. Now I see a clear road of getting out of this. I am going to engage a barrister, but instead of engaging a barrister tha can have the money if tha will come with me to Browne's place and swear that this is all false what Chapman says." In answer to what he was going to give witness, prisoner replied " I'll give thee three sovereigns, which 1 will put into John Cross's bands now. Then I shall want thee to go to Mr. Browne's place and swear that it is false. Theo John Cross shall give thee three sovereigns." Witness said that he , should do nothing of the kind.—lSathaniel Clarke. wheel- ' wright's apprentice, formerly in the employ of prisoner, ' spoke to helping to remove sled " distribute " property at Spann's premisQs before the public examination of the bankrupt. —John Cross, wood-turner, spoke concerning goods that were sent to his shop by prisoner. Witneas asked Spann why he had sent them. Spann replied that he had had a writ from Mr. Garland, , felt in a bit of trouble, and should file his petition. Wit- ness sent the goods back. Bridge came to witness's house, and Spann was sent for. He (Spans) asked what they 11 were going to do with Lim, and Bridge replied that he did not know. Spann said, "I suppose it is a money miltr with you," and Bridge answered, " Those who pty me best I will work for." He had lost 12 weeks' work, and Mr. Garland was going to pay him his wages. Spann said, "That will be £lB, and I can't afford that."—Joseph Crosst son of last witness, spoke to some shafts, wheels, a vice, a Paint mill, and other things being brought to his father's shop by Chapman and Bridge, and taken back by himself.— Joseph Ashton, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Wilderspool Causeway. and John Clarke, landlord of the Royal Oak Branch, Latchford, gave evidence to the efftct that various goods were brought to their premises, but were sent back to Spann's.—Prisoner, who reserved his defence, was com- mitted to the Assizes for trial, the Bench refusing to take lower bail than that Previously fixed—prisoner with £2OO, and two sureties of £lOO each. Prisoner was remanded in custody.

div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

by its daring is considered to surpass all his recent I' efforts. It is a protest against the esthetic greens ' which were at last finding their way even into Paris. The great Worth hates green as a colour, and of all greens he hates olive. But the taste for green was too strong for him, and having to yield to it he invented chartreuse and brought in apple green. These two at least staved off the olive arrangement, and having served that purpose he now decrees that they are unfashionable, and intro- duces his chocolate and cerise. I This great invention he has given to his public, but at the same time he introduced a novelty for his private behoof. Even in Paris an eminent man- milliner may be ruined in the midst of the greatest success. Mr. Worth discovered that all his illustri- ous customers did not pay their bills—there were some who could not, and there were some who would not. So he had a conference with his secre- tary; there was great examining of the books; other purveyors of fashionable luxuries to the leaders of Parisian ton were invited to attend, and in the re- suit something very practical was done. A list was compiled—indeed there were two lisd. There were I the customers who could not pay and there were I the customers who would not pay, and the 'great Mr. Worth would have no dealings with either. It I happened, unfortunately, that this list got about, and I hear that the wives of two journalists found their names in the index. There is great solidarity in the French press. They are all confreres and col- laboreteurs. It was a matter of chivalry and.polite- ness to stand by one another. And so, notwithstand- ing the cerise and the chocolate, the press has lately been rather down on the great milliner and dress designer, who has his own bills to meet and his own employes to pay, and has long stood the brunt of many bad debts. Perhaps in reducing his credit he will in future reduce also his prices:

LONDON, THNILSDA.Y. The level course of public affairs with a Conserva- tive Ministry acting under the surveillance of a Liberal majority has suddenly been disturbed by warlike rumours. The Russians, it is said, have advanced in force to Zulfikar, a pass which in accordance with the arrangements made with Russia by Mr. Gladstone's Government was secured to Afghanistan. At present this is merely a rumour, which Lord Randolph Churchill admits has reached the Government. The further statement that "it is believed Colonel Alikanhoff has determined to force on a war and is deceiving the Czar" goes some way towards discrediting the telegram, as in- dicating that its source is either purely alansnist •or directly connected with the Stock Exchange. What is anonymously " believed " to be the intention of Colonel Alikanhoff is scarcely a matter worth 'telegraphing at the rate of 4s. 6d. a word. If the late Government were in office this report might be passed over without anxiety. But with Lord , Salisbury in charge of foreign affairs, and Lord Randolph Churchill looking after India, matters assume a more serious aspect. The two Lords have for months cried aloud for war, and are now by chance in a position to precipitate it. Whether a sense of responsibility will sober them or not remains to be seen. In the meantime all stocks that could be effected by war with Russia have suddenly and decidedly dropped. Affairs in the House .of Commons are quietly pro- ceeding, though there is some sign of revolt on the Conservative side in the matter of the legislative ' intentions of the Government. The main policy of ministers, dearer to their hearts even than a war ' with Russia, is to maintain their places as long as ' possible, and with as little friction as may be., To I this end they prove most yielding to the demands! of the majority.
