div.head: "THE NATIONAL REFORM UNION AT ST. HELENS."
div.p: "THE NATIONAL REFORM UNION AT ST. HELENS."

Sir,—A letter under the above heading from two gentle- men using one pen, and the signature "A Probable Voter," appeared in your issue of last week. which I very much regret escaped my notice till this somewhat late date. Late as it is, will you, of your courtesy, allow me a word or two by way of explanation, and in reply to this dual voter ? This modern Damon and Pythias using ((or the moment) one umbrella and one signature seems mightily hurt that another agency for the dissemination of Liberal principles has been established in St. Helms. On the principle that you cannot have too much of a good thing, one would have thought that this would have given ClIl3O for rejoicing to Iwo such shining lights of Liberalism, instead of stirring them up to anger and evil speaking. We may regret this unexpected result of our action, but must be content to go oe our way in spite of the insane opposition of Messieurs Damon and Py t hias. The fact is, Sir, that this very tin' explosion is caused by disappointment on the part of our two censors, and not by easy concern they have for the Cause of Liberalism. It was seen and deplored by many that the "old institution in Hardshaw " was dozing out a lethargic existence under the Influence of such men as Messrs. D. and P., to the utter neglect of the very large class which it is the business of the National Reform Union to seek and (politically) save. What more natural than that the first thought of those who thought on the subject should have turned to that society which was to them much more easy of access than "the old institution in Hardshaw-street ?" Having done so, DO difficulty was found in establishing a branch its St. Helens, where, if in any constituency in England, such a branch was needed. The "bole and corner meetings" were only so to the new Damon and Pythias, who belong to the large class who sit patiently on the fence criticising the battle until victory is declared, and then calmly mingle with the victors, claiming their share of the spoil. The "vapouring imaginings" of the speakers are not the close reasoniogs and convincing arguments to be had hot and hot from the brain of a Damon or a Pythias, but what would you have? We cannot all emulate these gentlemen, but we give of our best; and when we deliver our own souls and satisfy our hearers we are content. The "promoters" (Messrs. D. and P. are still thinking on the new railway scheme) are, so far from "popularity-hunting." some of them giving up a much wid,r and better paying popularity for the sake of a cause they hare at heart, and that is the work they conscientiously believe to be lying nearest to their hinds. We may and do regret (some of us do at least) that this dual voter cannot see his way to give us his support; we shall try to rub along and survive without it. But you will probably permit me, Mr. Editor, to point out to "these two single gentlemen rolled into one" that the study of one's own navel is the least edifying of human studies. When, however, the student begins to imagine that he sees in this organ of his own body the real and only umbel of the universe, there is a grotesqueness about the matter that compels the bystander to laugh when tears would be pro- bably a more fitting tribute to this spectacle of human weakness and folly.—l am, dec., St. Helens, 15th July, 1885. THE SECRETARY.

div.head: EX A MTNER, SATURDAY, JULY 18, 1885
div.p: THE EX A MTNER, SATURDAY, JULY 18, 1885

"marsh" to Morley Common is stopped, and guarded by 1 Sir Gilbert's gamekeeper. This narrow piece of laod, al- I most entirely useless for the purposes of cultivation' only about one acre in extent, belongs to the Birkenhead Joint Railway. Company, and for at least 18 years the footpath across it has been open to the public as a means of access to Morley Common. It is a very pleasant little bye-path, and just one of those agreeable places which all irds variety, and consequently pleasure, to a man who strolls out for a quiet country walk. This bit of marsh land, however, is the breeding place of a few "snipe," which, I suppose, are "game." • • • . • • •• • • •

-There is nothing so sacred—l was almost saying " holy " —as "game" in the eye of the landowner: and as Sir Gilbert is, somehow or other, while not the owner of the land, still the owner of these miserable " snipe," he has persuaded the railway company to stop up the footpath. This action will deprive hundreds of people every week of i a most agreeable bit of, recreation, and by comptlling others i to go a considerable distance round to get to and from ! Warrington and Walton, will also be a source of great in- I convenience and annoyance. Sir Gilbert already has the I shooting over hundreds of acres of land as strictly pre- ' served as it is possible for gamekeepers and other landlords' minions to make it; but not content with that. he 'must lay his hands upon this strip of land for the sake of these' paltry birds. The pleasure and convenience of the hundreds ~of working people and others is as nothing to Sir Gilbert's selfish gratification in preserving this trifling bit of game. Men are judged not by their " words," but by their "deeds," and this action of Sir Gilbert's proclaims aloud the hollow- ness of his pretended anxiety for the well-being of the people of this neighbourhood. Men, women, and little children are pining daily in the cl ised up courts and alleys of our manufacturing towns for a breath of God's pore air, but if ever we are to realise the emancipition of " the common people" we must sweep away from amongst our legislators all those whose nature is warped and nat rowed by the selfishness begotten of bigotry and class privilege. Working-men, remember Morley Common.—Yours, PEDESTRIAN. Warrington, July 16th, 1885.

The Cereerceeton of the EXCFIEQUER, replying to Mr. J. Talbot, said he quite recognised the importance of se- I curing an efficient system of national education, and at the same time of preventing as far as possible undue pressure upon the ratepayers. He would, however, see whether something could not be done in that direction without ap- pointing a Royal Commission.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. Atkinson, said the produce of foreign farmers carried by English railways at less rates than English produce hardly came within the question of agricultural depression to be referred to a Royal Commis- stun, IRA he would consult the President of the Board of Trade on the subject.-Mr. BOURKE, replying to Mr. Rushtoo, sold negotiations between the Great Powers on the guarantee of the Egyptian nine million loan were still proceeding -The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. James Strtert, said the Medical Relief Disfranchisement Bill was the first order on Tuesday. The Government hoped the committee would be got through early, and then the Crimi- nal Law Amendment Bill would be proceeded with. CRIMINAL LAW IN IRELAND.—OR the motion to go into committee of supply, Mr. PARNELL called attention to the mal-adruinistration Of criminal law in Ireland, and more es- pecially certain provisions of the Crimes Prevention Act during the viceroyalty of Earl Spencer, whereby persons bad, I been, in some cases, condemned to death and executed, and , in others sentenced to penal servitude for life, or for a long I I term co! years, which sentence was tow going on. He said the late Government upheld Earl Spencer as a kind of Pope, who could do no wrong, but since then a change of Ad- ministration had taken place, and he hoped the inquiry he now asked for would be granted, and the prison doors , opened to men who were suffering for crimes they had not ' committed, and of which they knew nothing. If the state- ments he made were denied, that could only be successfully accomplished by producing the dying declaration of the unfortunate men which the late Government refused to do. Having gone at length into the circumstances of each case, he moved that in the opinion of that House it was the duty I of the Government to institute strict iuquiry into the evi- dence aed convictions in the Maamstrasna, Barbervilla, , Cross Magian, and Castle Island casee. He looked hope- fully to the new Government, and hoped his demand for 1 justice would not be refused.—The CHANCELLOR of the ExcnEctuEre said it would be for the convenience of the House if he at once stated the case Government would put- sue. There was very much in the policy of the late Government for which he should be sorry to be responsible, but as regarded the accusation that had been made against Lord Spencer by others not certainly by the member for Cork, in the speech he had just made, he be- lieved that nobleman quite incapable of the conduct impu- ted to him. On the contrary, he knew him to be an Eng- lish nobleman and an honourable man, and in all he had elone—he might have made mistakes—he had done nothing hut that he believed his duty. With regard to the resolu- tion of the hon. gentleman, such a proposal would be de- rogatory of the power and authority of the Lord-Lieu- tenant, and he must ask the House to resist it.—Sir. W. HARCOURT defended the action of the late Go- vernment, and said they were proud to be responsible for the action of Lard Spencer. He justified all that had been done, and denied that justice had b.SII ' un- fairly administered.—Lord R. CHURCHILL justified his vote against the resolution of Mr. Parnell, and urged the with- drawal of the resolution.—Mr. PARNELL asked leave to withdraw his resolution.—Mr. Hartutenerox at great length I went through the whole circumstances of the Maamtrasna I murders, the trial of the prisoners, ant the procedure at the trial.—Mr. C. LEWIS could not help remarking the peculiarly peaceful language of Mr. Parnell in asking leave to withdraw his resolution. To his mind it sheered clearly that if there was not a treaty, there was an understanding between him and the Government.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A telegram from Cork announces the departure of a great number of Munster Bank shareholders to attend the society's meeting its Dublin. The meeting, it is feared, will be a very stormy one. The Solect Committee on Admiralty expenditure and lia- bilities met on Friday for the first time, and appointed Mr. Goechen the chairman. The next sitting is on Monday, , when witnesses will be called. I WIFE MURDER—On Friday, at the Cardiganshire Assizes, before Mr. Justice Denman, John Price, labourer ' and Sergeant in the Cardiganshire Artillery Militia, was convicted ot the murder of his wife on the 29th May last. The prisoner was sentenced to death. I FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.—A fire broke out shortly after two o'clock on Friday morning at No. 4, White Horse Yard, Drury Lane, London, in premises occupied by Mrs. Crisp, a woman 60 years of age. The firemen soon subdued the flames, but on entering the building found that the un- fortunate woman had been suffocated. I SUPPOSED Loss OF & SHIP AND 30 LIVES —All hope has been abandoned of the safety of the four-masted ship County 1 of Aberdeen which, after landing a cargo of jute at Dundee, left Cardiff for Bombay on the 22nd December and has not since been reported. She was commanded by Captain Millar, of Aberdeen, and carried a crew of thirty hands, some of , whom belonged to Forfarshire. I COT TO PIECES ON THE RAILWAY.—A shocking fatality occurred on Friday morning at Bolton. A telegraph Ines- ' ssriver named George Harley Bousted, aged thirteen, was taking a message to the waggon works, near the Bury junc- tion At Bolton Station, on the Lancsshire and Yorkshire I Railway, when, on crossing the line, he was knocked down by the Blackburn and Manchester express and cut in two. Death was instantaneous. MR. GLADSTONE, who was unable to address the House of Commons on Thursday night has written a letter to Mr. Childers, in which he offers some criticism of Tory finance. , He points out that the whole of the new taxation is to be I supplied by Property, and believes that" the future force I of this precedent sapplied by a Tory Government will not be inconsiderable!' The Press Association is able to statepiat Mr. Gladstone is going on very well, the hoarse- ness being less apparent. • WIFE MURDER THROUGH JEALOUSY. At Hammer- smith, on Friday morning, Harry Norman, painter, living in Rvlston•road, Fulham, was charged with the wilful murder of his wife by stabbing her with a dagger. The , prisoner gave himself up at Fulham-road police station this I morning, saying he had killed his wife because she had L taken liberties with the landlord. An inspector proceeded to the house, and found the woman dead on the bed, with blood on the left breast and a bloodstained dagger near, The prisoner was remanded. THE EXTRAORDINARY ACTION BY & NUN.—The re- mark able action by Miss Dwyer, a novitiate in a London convent, against two neighbours for slandering her by asserting she left Ireland to hide her shame and, in London, gave birth to a child, concluded on Thursday evening at the Limerick Assizes. The Judge said the accusations made against the plaintiff on her return from the London convent with a rich sister, also a nun, were of shameful, immoral, and injurious conduct. No proof that she had been guilty of any impropriety while in the convent had been attempted. The jury gave the plaintiff £5O damages.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO PRESTON.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT TO PRESTON.

There was great excitement, especially among the work- ing people of Preston, on Friday morning, his Royal High- ness having consented to receive specimens of local made fabrics. The ceremony took place in the Public Hall, and the mill hands balloted for the places. The present of specimens woe enclosed in an ebony and gold case, 7 feet 6 inches high. It was placed near the dais. The ball being crowded the doors were closed at 10-15. His Royal High- ness arrived shortly before eleven, the Northamptonshire Regiment forming guard of honour at the station. There was the same escort as on the previous day, and the Prince was swain met by the Mayor, Lord Lieutenant, the High Sheriff, and other officials. He was enthusiasticlly received. At the Public Hall he was presented with an illuminated addrPss, which expressed the delight of the cotton operatives that th,. Prince had accepted some specimens of their labour. The condescension of his Royal Highness reminded them of the deep concern his Royal Highness had so long mani- fested in design and ingenuity of invention. The address also referred to the interest the late Prince Consort always manifested in the cotton trade of this country, which gave bread to so tinny millians of loyal subjects. His Royal Highness having replied, he proceeded to the Royal Agri- cultural Show.

The showyard was opened at nine o'clock. The morning being fine, there again promises to be an exceptionally large attendance. The number at three o'clock on Thursday was over 9,000 larger than the total at Shrewsbury at the close of the second day. The special prizes for implements and the medals offered by the society have not yet been awarded. Excursions have again arrived in the town from all parts of the country, and crowds flock on to the ground to have the doable privilege of seeing the Prince and the show. Miss Smithard, the demonstrator at the working dairy, which was visited by his Royal Highness on Thursday, delivered another lecture on Friday morning, and there are frequent illustrations of bee-driving at the tent.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. THURSDAY. Mr. W. E. Forster's committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill rnrt again on Thursday. Mr. Francis Stevenson, chief engineer to the London and North-Western Railway Company, examined by Mr. Moos, said that the proposed railway deviation would be an inter- ference with the traffic of the company, especially to Scot- land and the North, and would put the company to con- siderable expense. He looked with aporehension on the effect tute works would have upon Runcorn Bridge, which was the second largest of the kind in the kingdom. He also apprehended danger from the yardarms of vessels striking against the lattice work of the bridge. The canal would also interfere with their traffic at Liverpool-road Station. Manchester. The company had spent about £lOO.OOO on the docks at Garston. It was im- portant that nothing should be done which would interfere with the entrance to the docks, which were largely used by vessels for coaling purposes.— Mr. Rend al, civil engineer, said he had bad a great deal of experience is docks and river work. He had carefully con- sidered the promoters' plane, and it was his firm conviction that the works would destroy Garston as a port. It was his definite conviction that the whole of that side et the river would fill up.—Mr. Barry, CE., eximined by Mr. Littler, said he agreed with what had been Bald by the other en- gimeers as to the effect the proposed works would have upon the estuary and the bar at Liverpool.—Mr. J. B. Sumner, first-class pilot, of Liverpool, said he did not think any pru- dent master would undertake the risk of steaming up the Sloyne at a rapid speed. A strong wind across the canal would render a vessel very unhandy is steering.—Captain Billing, at present in command of the Great Eastern, and with 40 years' experience in the merchant service, said he had been 24 times through the Suez Canal, and twice through t,he Amsterdam Canal. It would be extremely dangerous to =deem into the entrance of the proposed locks, and a vessel 300 feet long could not swing with safety in the entrance.

div.head: FRIDAY.
div.p: FRIDAY.

Witnesses were called before the Select Committee on Friday to spealc to the alleged difficulty of navigeting the canal, after which the opponents opened their commercial case. Evidence was given that extra rates would be charged by shipowners for conveyance of goods to Manchester. Mr. MAson. who was formerly connected with the Great Northern stitrei his reasons for believing that the canal would be a financially unsound undertaking.

Telawrava, Tomr 3.—Admiral Miot, commineler•in- chief of the French forces in Madagascar, has had an inter- view with the Hoya asers, the result of which has not yet traospired. Preparation are being made for the ac- commodation of the French reinforcements which are shortly expected.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. - DEFENCE OF THE BRITISH COAST.—ESTI COWPER drew attention to the insufficiently defended condition of corn- •rnercial ports and seaside towns, and asked what measures the Government proposed to take.—The Earl of HAR. R0W134", in reply, said the First Lord of the Admiralty would shortly lay before his naval colleagues proposals for improving the cmdition of the ports in question. Toe enormous expense would render it impossible for the Gov- ernment to undertake harbour &fano% of all commercial parts. The Admiralty felt they must rely to a great ex- tent iiiffin localities for the serious part of the work, and the Government would do all they could to encourage a volun- teer movement. —in the discussion which followed, Lord NORTHBROOK expressed willivgness to support the Govern- ment in an improvement of the navy, but contended that the coast defences must rest with the artillery.—The Earl of MORLEY' expressed a similar opinion. IRISR LAND PURCHASE B ILL.—Lord ASEMORNE presen- ted a hill to provide greater facilities for the sale of land to occupying tenants in Irelstm. The bill would provide for the advance of three-fourths of the purchase money to , those who desind a limited advance, and also advance of the whole purchase money at four per cent., repayable in for!y-nine years, Government retaining one-fifth as a guarante. The Government would also employ Irish church surplus to save the State from possible loss.—Earl SPENCER spoke si the urgent necessity of the settlement of the land question in Ireland, and promised the bill should be errefully considered by the Opposition.—Lord Asn- BOURNE, replying to the question, said it was proposed to limit the advances under the bill to five millions, and the I ' Government might advance that atm all in one year.—ln
LIBERAL MEE EING AT RUNCORN.

The present series of Liberal Ward meetings were brought t6an end last evening, when Mr. J. T. Brunner addressed a meeting of the electors of the Duke's Field Ward. Mr. W. H. Chadwick presided, and there was a good attendance. He was supported on the platform by Messrs. B. Kniveton, J. D. Jones, and 0. Leak (secretary).—After a short intro- ductory speech by the Chairman, Mr. Brunner addressed the electors. H 3 did not think much of Mr. Verdin as a politician, and his invective, like that of " my Lord Salis- bury's." certainly wanted finish. Mr. Verdin did not know bow these county boards were going to be constituted, but he was very glad that my Lord Silishury bad spoken so freely upon the subject. (Laughter.) What were they to say about this one political idea which Mr. Verdin had been good enough to give them for their edification ? Alluding to the cumbersome mode of procedure by which business in the House of Commons was managed, Mr. Brunner said Mr. Gladstone by his system of Grand Com- mittees bad taken a step forward in the direction of freeing the House of Commons. He did not go in for the abolition of a Second Chamber. (Hear, hear.) He did not wish that it should cease to be called the House of Lords, but he wished that the hereditary principle should be abolished. (Applause.) A friend had spoken about "Modern Baby- lon." He did not know whether it would be to their Pleasure that he should sfay a few words upon the question. (Applause.) It was a question which was filling the hearts and minds of the people of this country with a rapidity such as be bad no conception of 14 days ao. Since he bad read the burning words in the Pall Mall Gazette this horrible state of affairs in London had possessed him like a night mare, and he had made up his mind that wherever he met a fellow man he would strive to induce him to join him in a crusade against it. (Applause.) Ha meant to ask them to instruct the chairman to send a peti- tion which he would ask Mr. Leak to draw up, to the House of Commons to Amend the Criminal Law Amendment Bill now before Parliament. (Applause.)-0n the motion of Mr. J.. 1) Jones, seconded by Mr. B. Kniyeton. and supported by Captain Le Ceutier. a resolution to support Mr. Brunner Was carried enthusiastically.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OE DR. MOURITZ, OF
RUN CORN.

Dr. Robert Unhurt Mouritz surgeon, High-street, Run- corn, died on Sunday morning last, at his residence, after an illness extending over several months. 1 he fleceasetl gentle- man, who was the second son of Mr. Robert Mouritz, of Mount Bailie, Coenty Louth, Inland, was born in Nove.n- ber, 1821, Being intended for the medical profeseion he commenced, after a successful scholastic career, his studies at the County Louth Infirmary, end subsequently he pre- ceeded to Dublin, where he obtained his diploma from the Royal College of Surgeons. He was at one time medic4l officer in charge of the missionary eettlemeat in Achil Island, and on his return to England he took up his resi- dence in Runcorn in 1864, succeding to the practice of the late Dr. Wilson. In that year he was appointed surgeon to the local corps of the 2nd C.R.V.. and on his retirement three years ago, he was allowed to retain his commission of surgeon major. Besides being surgeon to several local friendly societies, and certifying surgeon under tho Factory Acts for Runcorn and Widnes, he hid the important post of medical officer to the Board of Improvement Commis- sioners, which appointoseet he held for a period of 17 years. In all these positions he acted in a painstaking and con- scientious manner, and he was hell in the highest respect by a large circle of acquaintances and friends. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon, at the Cemetery Green- way-road. The cortege left High-street about three o'clock. In front were the following representatives of the Board of Commissioners ;—Messrs. R. Shaw (chairman), S. Taylor, H. White, W. Whittaker, HI J. Grice, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), M. Barker (surveyor), E. Marshall (secretary), c, Dutton (market superintendent), and J;Percival (inspector of nuisances). Mr. F. A. Lake would have been present out was detained in an action at the County Court Next cants Messrs. T. Simister, W Garnett, W. Pendlehury, John Mel- ler, Joseph Cook, Thomas Harrison, John Pendlebury, and Jos. Hallsworth (representing the Deke'e Club), W. Haejejn. son,W. Sutton' W. Brooke,And Dr. Robineon. The carriages of Mrs Hazlehnrst and Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., followed, the Rev. R. Edwards and Dr. McDougall occupying seats in the former. The mourning coaches succeeding. the he ,re contained Dr. John Mouritz, Dublin (brother); Mr. A. M. Dunlop, London (eon-in-law); Mr. Frank Mouritz, B.A. (nephew); and Mr. John Cox. At the cemetery the body was met by the Revs. Came Barclay, M.A., J. j. Bryant, M.A., Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., Captain Haziehinst, J.P., and Mr. A. F. Brundrit. The coffin bore the follow- ing inscription :—" Robert H. Mouritz, died July 12, 1885, aged 63. Nothing in my hand I bring, simply to Thy cross I cling." Wreaths and floral crosses were sent and placed on the coffin by Mrs and Miss Mouritz, Mrs A. M. Dunlop, Mr. S. B. and Mrs Chadwick, Mrs C. Hszlehurst, Miss Bar- clay, Miss A. Rougier, Mrs Barker, Mr. J. Brundri% and Captain Hazlehurst. The burial service was read by the Rey. R. Edwards (carats in charge of Newtown Mission.) For the present the practice of the late Dr. Mouritz will be continued by Dr. Anebro. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TUESDAY —Before Hls Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. THE LlST.—There were 163 plaints, 18 judgment sum- monses, and 3 adjourned plaints set down for hearing. BAKERS AND THEIR BREAD.—George Cameron, haker, Parr, St. Helens, sued Mary Collier, grocer and provision Idealer, Church-street, Runcorn, for £3, being 311 s wages alleged to be due, and 30e damages for wren.eful dismissal. Mr. J. 0. Swift, St. He:ens, appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant was represented by Mr. F. A. Like. The facts of the case, which lasted about three hours. were shortly these. The plaintiff was crigigeel by the defendant at a salary of 303 per week, arid on the 2.5 th April 1:e was discharged without notice, on the ground that he spoiled Op bread. He admitted that he had spoiled one batch through his assistant not turning tr.) at his proper time, and he understood from Mrs Collier on that UCCASiOII that he had done as well as he could under the cycametances. The bread ho baked was good. considering the quality of t'.e flour. Thomas Burroughs, baker in tne em- ploy of the Runcorn Co-operative Society. and William Jones, in the employ of Mr. R. Gorst, baker, Runcorn, were ex maned. They had seen some of the bread, which was l good for the price-4d a loaf—and as good as could be made l out of the flour used, namely, one sack of Lewis's to one sack of Fairelough's. This mixture was out of propertion, the usual quantities being 0143 sick of Lewis's to seven of Fairclough's.—For the defence, Walter Col- lier, drfenclint's manager, and Miss Collier iver. called, and stated that the plaintiff Spoiled en an

average a batch of bread a week, during the time he was employed with the defendant. When told hie services would be required no longer by W. Collier, he said he hoped they would give him a reference and put nothing in it that would be detrimental to hi a characti-r„ because if it were stated that he was incompetent he would not be able to get the assistance of the Bakers' Society. He made the same request to Miss Collier, who declined to agree to it. She said if he liked she would simply state that he bad left without giving the reason. She wrote and sealed him a reference, but he opened it in her preeenco and then tore it up. Several witnesses proved that the bread was often sour.—His Honour held that the plaintiff was a com- petent baker, and therefore had ne excuse for spoiling the bread. Under the circumstances the defendant Was justified in discharging him. Judgment for the defendant with costs.

CONTEMPT OF COUBT.—William Blyth, clothier, High, street, sued James Jones of Vine-street, for Li 123 03d for goods supplied. Mr. Jones, Burton appeared for the plaintiff.—His Honour, after hearing the evidence, gave a verdict for the plaintiff, whereupon the defendant said "I'll never pay it." His Honour immediatav ordered the man into custody, and st the conclusion of the business severely reprimanded him telling him that ke must treat the court with respect or he should certainly commit him to geel for contempt.—The defendant apologised and was permitted to leave the court.

ISr. HELENS WATERWORHS.-011 Thursday the Water iCommittee of the St. Helens Corporation made their annual inspection of the various pumping stations and other works I connected with the water supply of the town. The nv-m- -hers who started on Thursday morning were the Mayor P(Alderman Cook), Alderman Mcßryde (chairman of c.on- mittee), Councillors Foster and Wilcock, Mr. D. M. F. Gaskin, C.E. (engineer), and Mr. J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk). The committee expressed themselves satisfied with the machinery at the Collins Green, Sutton-road, and ' Eccleston Hill, and lirhiston stations, but with regard to the buildings at the latter place, early atention, they consi- dered. should be given to their renovation. ,•• "AFTER His KITE" IN A CONSTABLE'S GARDEN. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Albert Jones, 11 veers of age, residing at Wargrave, was summoned for dem- iaging a garden hy trespassing, in the occupation of P.C. McMullen. The defendant pleaded not guilty. P.C. McMullen said that the defendant's father and mother re- sided next door to his station at .Wergraye. On the afrer• noon of Saturday, the 27th ult, he eaw the defendant fly• in?, a kite in his garden. He damaged the cabbeg:s end rhubarb to the artunent of id at the least. Ile called to tile lad to come out ;.1.- the garden, but for a time he took no notice of it.—Mr.l'3,ones, defmdant's father, stated that when his son was flyfteg his kite the string caught on a hedge and the lad wen and released it. There was no ,damage at all done.—Tie o Bench ordered the defendant's father to pay the costs and the damage.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

WE LEARN that our townsman, Mr. J. 31. Muir, has just passed a successful examination at the College of Organists, London, and thus becomes an Associate of that college. We observe in the Times of tho 4th July the name of Mr. James Lyon Whittle among those of the suc- cessful candidates at the solicitor's final examina- tion held on the 16th and 17th June last.

TILE MARKET. -- The work of completing the hitherto open portion of the market has been finished, and the whole is now covered, the size and arrangements of the market being admirable. • ROUNDERS' CUM.—A club match was played on Saturday and Monday evening, on the practice grounds, between Captain's and Secretary's teams, resulting in the victory of the latter by nine runs. TRANSFERS.—The Borough Magistrates, on Mon- day, sanctioned the transfers of the Hope -Qole Inn, Horsemarket-street, from James Hill to George Bradshaw, and of the Stamford Arus, Stamford- street, from Peter Woodhall to James Lockett.

ACCIDENT.—A boy named John Rigby (2), son of Thomas Rigby, file cutter, Orchard-street, was knocked down and run over on Saturday evening in Church-street. The boy had wandered into the street and was knocked down by a four-wheeled vehicle that was passing. He had a narrow escape of being killed, but fortunately does not seem to have been very much injured. SUDDEN DRATH.—Henry Davies (64), a painter, who lived at 34, King-street, died suddenly on Tuesday morning. 'Deceased, who was subject to rheumatism, had of late been unwell, but he fol- lowed his occupation up to Saturday. On Tuesday morning he complained of his throat being bad and stayed in bed. About eleven o'clock his landlady went to the room and found him on the floor dead. He had apparently risen with the in,tention of dress- ing. THE BIRTH AND DEA.TH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week eliding Saturday, July llth, 1885.—The mean temperature was 58 Fahr., and therefore 'll degrees warmer than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 72 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 7th inst., and the minimum temperature. 44 Fahrenheit, on the 9th inst.. • The rainfall measured half an inch. The general direction of the -wind Was W. During the week, which was the 28th of the current year, 38 births and 11 deaths were registered.. The death rate from all causes was equal to 125 per 1,000, against 15.1 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 21 the cor- responding week of last year. The' deaths included 1 from typhoid fever, 3 from plithisis, 2 from brain disease, 1 from lung disease, 1 from kidney disease, 1 from heart disease, and one from old age. One case of typhoid fever, 1 of relapsing fever, 1 of measles and 5 of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.— Jonx H. GORNALL, Medical Office. of Health. FATAL AccinENT.--Last week ' a married man named John Thomason, of Oliver-street, fell from a building and fractured his arm. He was taken home, and on Monday lockjaw commenced and he was removed to the Infirmary, where Ile died on Tuesday afternoon. On Thursday afternoon Mr. W. T. Hus- band, deputy coroner, held an inquiry relative to the occurrence at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey- street. From the evidence of Robert Cook, finger and slater, 21, Allen-street, it appeared that deceased was employed by him as a labourer, and on the 7th linst. was working at some old buildings in Crown and Sceptre Yard. While so engaged he missed his footing when crossing some uncovered joists, and fell on to the pavement beneath, a distance of about ten feet. His ,arm was broken, and, according to further evidence called, he was taken to the Infir- mary and had his wound dressed. He remained an out-patient until Monday last, when lockjaw set in. ' He then became an in-patient and was attended by two doctors, but he died on Tuesday afternoon.— The jury returned a verdict to the effect, that the death of the deceased was caused by the after effects of an accident.

A FOOLISH Gil:L.—At the Borough Court, on Wed- nesday, a girl named Mary Wright (17), domestic servant, daughter of George Wright, Ilopkin's- road, was charged with stealing four yards of twill and seven yards of chintz, from the house of Samuel Dodd, chemical works labourer, New-road, Latch- ford, on or about the 24th ult. Prisoner, it was explained by Chief Constable Hunt, stayed at Dodd's for a week or ten days, and after she had left the articles were missed. They were afterwards found to have been pawned by prisoner, who now told the magistrates that she got 2s advanced on them, and spent is 6d in household necessaries, which she gave to Mrs. Dodd, gave 2d to Mrs. Dodd's child, and spent 3d on sweets, the remain- ing id being charged for the ticket at the pawn- shop. She bought them at the Salvation Army Stores.—Alderman Pickincre : Is she one of the Salvation Army ?—Prisoner: I used to be, but am not now.—The girl's father told the Court that when out of a situation she had been living with someone Connected with the Army, but he did not know where.—The Bench, after reprimanding pri- soner, decided to allow her to go, simply recording a conviction against her. A FIGHT I'oll A HUSBAND--At the Borough Court, yesterday, John Ford and Emma Bramball were charged with assaulting Ann Ford, the wife of the former, on Tuesday night. Mr. A. Browne, in- structed by John Ford's employer, appeared for that person.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) said that com- plainant was the wife of John Ford, and Bramhall was a woman with whom Ford had cohabited for years. Mrs. Ford had often complained of being abused by Bramhall in the street, and had caused the police and magistrates some trouble. On the night in question Mrs. Ford met the female prisoner near the Central Station, and, after using improper language to her, Struck and beat her about the head with a stone. The male prisoner, a witness would say, incited his paramour to continue the attack, and "give it her."—Complainant, in her evidence, said her husband had been a murderer ever since he cohabited with Mrs. Bramhall.--Mr.- Browne: You are the woman who sold her children to the gypsies, are•you not ?—Prisoner Ford: Yes, she did do.--Mr. Browne submitted that Ford had been forced to leave his wife through her misconduct, and that she had continued to annoy him ever since.--Bramball was sent to prison for a month and Ford ordered to be bound over, himself in £lO, and one surety of £5. ,

A WARNING.,---A system of sending notices. to creditors, apparently emanating from the Warring- ton County Court, by whin people ignorant of the ! law may be deceived, if not, indeed, intimidated, was exposed at a -sitting or that Court on Thursday, when a.woman appeared in Court with one of the notices, which his Honour Judge Ffoulkes said was a false one, and one of Which no notice should. be I taken The Registrar (Mr. Nicholson) said that there had been two such cases, and the Judge had directed him to communicate with tke Incorporated Law Society to see if something could not be done to put a stop to the system. The forms were printed ones, with nameS, addresses, and dates filled in in ink. One of them read: "Application before' proceeding in the County Court of Lancashire, holden at Warrington. Between John .Potter, Orford-lane, fitter, debtor, and Richard Travis, credi- tor. You are to fake notice that unless yon pay to '1 the undersigned on or before the '4th day of july ! itist ant, the sum of £0 us 4d, moneys owing by you to him, that legal proceedings will be instituted against you in the above County Court for the re-, covery thereof without further notice or delay. Signature : Richard Travis ; business : provision dealer; addresS : Warrington ; debt : us 4d ; ex- penses Dated this second day of July, in the year of our Lord 1885." In one corner of the docu- ment is the imprint "Messrs. Jones and Co.; Law Stationers.": The second form was similar with the exception of the tames, which were Mr,. Edward Heesoin, debtor, and Margaret Ellen Hackett. cre- ditor.

In the. first stage of the contest of the Queen's Prize all failed to score a sufficisnt number of points tO entitle them to take part in the second stage. Their score were:- 200 500 600 _,T°- yes. yds. yds. ur; Lance-Corporal Wright Oorpol al Sutton 2l 22 18 Lance-Sergeant Bat-.man 24 29 25 RAILWAY ACCIDENTS AT ST HELENS STAT/ON.--- On Friday night, a singular accident occurred at St. Helenti railway statinn. When the train from Lime-street station had arrived and the pisriengers alighted on the main plat' form, the train was being shunted into a siding, which in' clines towards the waiting rooms. Toe break was aPPlie4 by a porter, bait it did not act. and the rellult, was that the train rushed with such great force into the stop blocks that nearly all the buffers and windows on the carriage.° were smashed. On the following morning the damage°, carriages were despatched for repairs to the compallT! works at Wolverton. Another accident occurred at tb- .Station on Tuesday afternoon. About five o'clock a shire and and Yorkshire train was being drawn from a siding into the station when the wheels of the engine struck paints under Raven-street bridge and threw the engine 04` the line. The first and two last carriagss kept the rails, but the second one was thrown off. The two last coaches Were brought on the main line, the bank engine attached tOW: and the Ormskirk and f'outhport passengers were despatcbea to their destination about 15 minotes behind time. A break' down gang from Sutton speedily got to work, and at a quarter to eight the engine was placed in its proper positiOn and started homewards. About a month ago, it is stated, another engine belonging to the same company was thrown off the line at the R4GIS paints. • A FATHEIt'S RIGHT TO CHASTI.E HIS DalfenTralt• —ExTBAOHDIBARY Casa.—At the Newton Petty Sessionn on Saturday, before Colonel McCnrquodale, Messrs. Houghton. C. Pilkington, A. C:MeCorgrodale, and W. Fr, Gooch, Martin Nalley, of Golborne, was entnmonea for committing 3 breach of the peace.—The de- , fondant said he wonld plead guilty to striking bis slrfa. daughter.—P.C. Ratcliffe said that at twenty minutes Pio' eight on the night of the 4th inst. be was on duty in Hie street. The defendant's daughter Was passing along LI street, when the defendant rushed out of Heatn-street an began beating his daughter with a bdt. He struck ber ahout the head and shoulders, and he alee threatened te assault one or two other persons who interfered.
